question: Does prayer here mean the ritual act, the mosque, or both?

positions.position: Prayer and mosque
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): The mosque reading answers that people ordinarily go to the mosque for prayer, so whatever prevents prayer also counts as a reason not to go to the mosque. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (ابن عباس وابن مسعود والحسن والشافعي): Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and al-Ḥasan take ‘prayer’ to mean the mosque, and al-Shāfiʿī adopts this view; it can mean ‘place of prayer’ by common ellipsis, as ṣalawāt means prayer sites at 22:40. | mentions 22:40 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (طائفة): Another group takes the wording to include both prayer and its place, since people then went to the mosque only for prayer and prayed only in congregation. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (الشافعي): If prayer means mosques, those passing through are allowed to cross while junub; al-Shāfiʿī holds this view. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (الشافعى): Al-Shafiʿi takes prayer to mean mosques: a junub person may not enter one except to pass through when needed. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī takes prayer to mean both the prayer itself and its place, the mosque: the verse bars an intoxicated person from praying and a sexually impure person from being in the mosque. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الضحاك وعكرمة والحسن): Al-Dahhak, Ikrima, and al-Hasan say prayer means its locations, by a state-for-place metaphor; the verse bars an intoxicated person from approaching a mosque out of reverence. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): Al-Shafi'i applies prayer to both the ritual act and its locations to accommodate both interpretations; al-Alusi rejects this because it combines literal and metaphorical senses. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (بعض المفسرين): Some commentators take salat here to mean the mosque or prayer-place, so the prohibition bars drunk people from entering mosques. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): On the mosque-passage interpretation, prayer means the act of worship for the intoxicated, but the mosque as the place of prayer for the junub. FARRA (source note FARRA:v1p268/r10) supports this position. MAJAZ (source note MAJAZ:v1p126/r8) supports this position. TAB-FULL (source note TAB-FULL:v7p53/r7) supports this position. IBNABIHATIM (source note IBNABIHATIM:v3p959/r1) supports this position. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (source note WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:43-44/r1) supports this position. JISHUMI (source note JISHUMI:v2p1567/r2) supports this position. JISHUMI (source note JISHUMI:v2p1567/r3) supports this position. KASHSHAF-FULL (source note KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p545#2/r3) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p56#2/r8) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p56#2/r9) supports this position.

positions.position: Ritual prayer
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (علي، مجاهد، الحكم، قتادة، ابن زيد، مقاتل، الفراء، الزجاج): One interpretation permits a traveler without water to perform tayammum and pray while junub; on this view, passing by means being a traveler and approaching prayer means performing it. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): If ṣalāt means the prayer, the verse bars praying drunk or junub except for a traveling wayfarer, allowing a junub traveler unable to find water to pray by tayammum. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الأكثرون): The majority take ṣalāt here to mean the prayer itself: do not perform it while intoxicated. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa takes 'prayer' to mean the ritual act itself, with 'until you know what you say' supporting that reading. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): Alternatively, there is no ellipsis: the prohibition concerns approaching prayer itself in this state. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (التيسير): Taysir says the prayer itself is not forbidden, since it is worship; rather, one must not become intoxicated so as to be unable to pray properly. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Most interpreters understand prayer as the specific ritual act; approaching it means rising to perform it and entering into it, with the wording intensifying the prohibition.

positions.position: Mosque or prayer place
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): If ṣalāt means the mosque, the verse bars entering it drunk or while junub except to pass through, allowing a junub person to cross the mosque, as al-Shāfiʿī holds. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أصحاب الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī’s adherents prefer the mosque reading because ‘approach’ naturally applies to a place, whereas it does not literally apply to the prayer itself. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أصحاب الشافعي): They argue the exception works under the mosque reading; under the prayer reading it fails because a sick nontraveler unable to use water may still pray by tayammum. BURHAN, d. 794 (author): In the prohibition on approaching prayer while intoxicated or impure, ṣalāt means the prayer itself in “until you know what you say,” but its place in “except as passersby.” BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): “Do not approach prayer” means do not enter the place where it is performed, much less perform the prayer itself. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The mosque reading is supported by a report that mosques should be kept away from children and madmen, but the phrase about knowing what one says weighs against it. STUDYQURAN (author): Ṣalāh or ṣalawāt can mean the place of prayer as well as prayer itself. | mentions 22:40 STUDYQURAN (Q): Clay can serve as a place of prayer, and its elements, water and earth, purify ritually; fire instead is a means of punishment in the Hereafter. | mentions 4:43, 5:6

question: What does intoxicated mean here?

positions.position: Wine intoxication
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (الجمهور): Most exegetes say the intoxication is from wine. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (جمهور الصحابة والتابعين): The majority of Companions and Successors understand the word as intoxication from wine, the opposite of sobriety. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور): The majority of scholars and jurists understand the intoxication here as intoxication from wine. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): A drinking poem plays on السكر as a stoppage or drunkenness in the phrase نداوي السكر بالسكر. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The command follows worship, filial kindness, good conduct, condemnation of miserliness, and the afterlife digression: prayer needed protection from wine’s disruption. | mentions 4:36, 4:37, 4:42 ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الجمهور): The majority understand سكارى as intoxicated from wine. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): The root sense of السكر is closure: intoxication blocks the link between a person and reason; the term usually means loss of reason through drink, but can also describe anger, love, and similar causes. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): The cited line’s repeated سكر witnesses metaphorical intoxication by love alongside literal wine intoxication. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Intoxication means loss of reason through wine or another cause; weakened reason lets Satan prompt the tongue toward verbal shirk even while the heart remains faithful, a statement that will cause anguish at judgment. STUDYQURAN (author): The four passages progress from wine as provision (16:67), to mixed benefit and sin (2:219), avoiding prayer while drunk here, and finally complete prohibition (5:90). | mentions 16:67, 2:219, 5:90 TAB-FULL (source note TAB-FULL:v7p45#2/r2) supports this position. positions.position: Sleep or drowsiness
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (الضحاك وأبو جعفر): Another view takes intoxication to mean sleepiness; Aisha reports the Prophet told a drowsy worshipper to leave in case he unknowingly prayed against himself. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet said that when someone grows drowsy during prayer, they should sleep until the drowsiness passes, lest they seek forgiveness while actually cursing themselves; al-Ḍaḥḥāk uses this to support the sleep interpretation. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Al-Rāzī prefers wine intoxication: sakr literally means drunkenness from wine, while intoxication from passion, anger, fear, or sleep is figurative and normally qualified; he cites 50:19 and 22:2. | mentions 50:19, 22:2 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak understands the state as sleepiness, citing the Prophetic direction that a sleepy worshipper should rest until alert because he may not know what he says. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi says the sleep and urinary-need interpretations express a sound principle: prayer requires wholehearted attention, free of distractions such as sleep, urgency, hunger, or anything that occupies and unsettles the mind. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): سكر is blocked discernment from intoxicating drink, likened to an eye covered by sleep or a river whose channels are blocked. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (القرطبي): Al-Qurṭubī says prayer requires heart and body engagement, so sleep, urinary pressure, hunger, and other distractions should be removed. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk interprets the phrase as drowsy from sleep, citing the Prophet’s instruction to sleep if drowsiness impairs prayer. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (الضحاك): Al-Dahhak interprets the intoxication here as sleepiness, not wine intoxication; Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmit this view. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (جعفر والضحاك وابن عباس): Ja'far, al-Dahhak, and one report from Ibn Abbas take intoxication here to mean overpowering sleep or drowsiness. question: How is junub formed and used?

positions.position: One form applies across genders and numbers
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Junuban is coordinated with the preceding circumstantial phrase and means a plural group; abiri sabil is an accusative exception. TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Junub applies to male or female, singular or plural, describing a person in janaba. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj notes that junub has the same form for one man, two men, and a group, as raḍī does. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa reads the junub traveler passing through as a traveler without water, who performs dry ablution and prays. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The forms تجنبتم, أجنبتم, and جنبتم all convey becoming junub; junub is generally indeclinable for gender, number, and plurality as a verbal noun-like form, though variants exist. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Some Arabic usage pluralizes junub as أجناب, like عنق/أعناق and طنب/أطناب; those who use جانب for the singular say جناب in the plural, like راكب/ركاب. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد وإسحاق): Aḥmad and Isḥāq allow a junub to sit in the mosque after performing ablution, according to Ibn al-Mundhir. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أصحاب الرأي): The adherents of raʾy allow a traveling junub to perform tayammum, enter a mosque to draw water from its spring, and leave with it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الثوري وإسحاق بن راهويه): Al-Thawrī and Isḥāq ibn Rāhwayh say a junub may cross a mosque only when necessary, after performing tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عطاء بن يسار): ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār reports that some Companions who became junub performed ablution, then came to the mosque and conversed there. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Junuban coordinates with the circumstantial clause “while you are intoxicated”; janub applies to all genders and numbers like a verbal noun. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Junub has the same form for singular and plural and for masculine and feminine because it functions like the verbal noun ijnāb. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī says junub has one form for singular and plural and for masculine and feminine, like the verbal noun ijnaab; Abū Ḥayyān calls it fluent, Qurʾānic usage and notes plural forms جنبون، أجناب and dual جنبان. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أحمد وإسحاق): Aḥmad and Isḥāq allow a junub who has performed ablution to sit in the mosque. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (علي): A second interpretation attributed to Ali takes the exception to mean a traveler who becomes junub and lacks water may perform prayer until water is available; reports from Ibn Abbas in one version, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and others say likewise. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو حنيفة ومالك والشافعي): Abu Hanifa, Malik, and al-Shafi‘i hold that a junub person may not remain in a mosque until bathing, or performing tayammum if water is unavailable or unusable. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أحمد): Ahmad permits a junub person to remain in the mosque after performing wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عطاء بن يسار): Ataa ibn Yasar saw Companions sitting in the mosque while junub after performing prayer wudu; Ibn Kathir calls this report sound on Muslim’s criteria. BURHAN, d. 794 (author): Singular forms also occur in descriptions of groups, including junub, ẓahīr, najiyy, and the generic singular al-ṭifl. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujahid says a junub person or menstruant may not pass through a mosque; the verse instead permits the traveler who lacks water to perform tayammum and pray. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says a person with smallpox, wounds, or ulcers who becomes junub and fears dying from bathing may perform tayammum. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Junub denotes a person in janaba after emission; it can be used as a singular noun or a plural. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): “Wa-lā junuban” is coordinated with the circumstantial clause “while you are intoxicated”; its accusative form confirms that the circumstantial clause occupies an accusative position. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): As a verbal-noun adjective, junub does not take a plural form even though it describes a plural subject. AKHFASH (source note AKHFASH:v1p258/r3) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p312/r7) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p312/r8) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p312/r9) supports this position. JISHUMI (source note JISHUMI:v2p1565/r7) supports this position. BAGHAWI-FULL (source note BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p219#2/r1) supports this position. BAGHAWI-FULL (source note BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p219#2/r2) supports this position.

positions.position: Derived from distance
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (ابن قتيبة): Ibn Qutayba says junub derives from distance or separation. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The root sense is distance: major emission leaves the person distant from the state required for prayer. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Junub is invariant in the eloquent language across gender and number, though some Arabs inflect it; Abu al-Baqa derives it from separation.

question: What makes someone junub?

positions.position: Emission or penetration makes one junub
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): ʿĀʾisha reports the Prophet ruled that ghusl is obligatory when the circumcised parts touch after intercourse. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو هريرة): Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet made ghusl obligatory after intercourse, with Muslim adding that this applies even without emission. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن القصار): Ibn al-Qaṣṣār says later generations of scholars agreed to follow the report about the two circumcised parts, ending the earlier disagreement. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور من الأمة): The majority define a junub as one impure through emission or penetration of the circumcised parts. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبي بن كعب): Ubayy reports that the Prophet instructed a man who had intercourse without emission to wash the affected area, perform ablution, and pray. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The author aligns with the scholars of the community: ghusl becomes obligatory upon penetration of the circumcised parts, whether or not emission occurs. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Junub refers to emission of semen, actual or near at hand through the meeting of the circumcised parts; it applies whether semen results from intercourse or otherwise. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The wording is agreed to signify intercourse, specifically the meeting of the circumcised parts, which requires ghusl. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The endpoint forbids prayer while junub until washing; since prayer is never waived, the verse establishes ghusl as obligatory. BAGHAWI-FULL (source note BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p221/r1) supports this position. BAGHAWI-FULL (source note BAGHAWI-FULL:v2p221/r2) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r10) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r11) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r12) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p57/r13) supports this position.

positions.position: Ghusl is due only after emission
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (بعض الصحابة): Some Companions held that ghusl is required only after emission, citing the report that water is due from water.

question: What does washing after janābah require?

positions.position: the maliki school differs over whether moving a ring and rubbing between the fingers are obligatory
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (أهل المذهب): The Maliki school differs over whether moving a ring and rubbing between the fingers are obligatory. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p319/r6) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p319/r7) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p319/r8) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p319/r9) supports this position. WAHIDI-WAJIZ (source note WAHIDI-WAJIZ:4:43-44/r5) supports this position.

positions.position: abū al-faraj cites a report that water must reach beneath every hair and the skin be thoroughly cleaned, which he takes to support rubbing
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو الفرج عمرو بن محمد المالكي): Abū al-Faraj cites a report that water must reach beneath every hair and the skin be thoroughly cleaned, which he takes to support rubbing.

positions.position: abū ʿumar argues that arabic can call either rubbing with water or pouring water a washing; ablution and ghusl may therefore be independent forms, not analogized to each other
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عمر): Abū ʿUmar argues that Arabic can call either rubbing with water or pouring water a washing; ablution and ghusl may therefore be independent forms, not analogized to each other.

positions.position: sufyān ibn ʿuyayna instead interprets cleaning the skin as washing and cleaning the genitals, not rubbing the whole body
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (سفيان بن عيينة): Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna instead interprets cleaning the skin as washing and cleaning the genitals, not rubbing the whole body.

positions.position: muslim records from ʿāʾisha and umm qays that the prophet poured water on a child after it urinated without rubbing, an analogy supporting sufficiency of pouring
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة وأم قيس بنت محصن): Muslim records from ʿĀʾisha and Umm Qays that the Prophet poured water on a child after it urinated without rubbing, an analogy supporting sufficiency of pouring.

positions.position: the majority hold that complete water coverage by pouring or immersion suffices for ghusl, without rubbing, based on reports describing the prophet's bath
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور من العلماء): The majority hold that complete water coverage by pouring or immersion suffices for ghusl, without rubbing, based on reports describing the Prophet's bath.

positions.position: ibn al-ʿarabī criticizes abū al-faraj, saying mālik never expressly or by inference held that ghusl without rubbing sufficed and that this was abū al-faraj's error
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabī criticizes Abū al-Faraj, saying Mālik never expressly or by inference held that ghusl without rubbing sufficed and that this was Abū al-Faraj's error.

positions.position: abū ʿumar says the mālik report explicitly validates immersion without rubbing or ablution, while the well-known mālikī position requires rubbing by analogy with ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عمر): Abū ʿUmar says the Mālik report explicitly validates immersion without rubbing or ablution, while the well-known Mālikī position requires rubbing by analogy with ablution.

positions.position: mālik, al-ṭabarī, al-layth, al-awzāʿī, and others do not require mouth or nose rinsing in ghusl or ablution because these are internal parts
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Mālik, al-Ṭabarī, al-Layth, al-Awzāʿī, and others do not require mouth or nose rinsing in ghusl or ablution because these are internal parts.

positions.position: ibn abī laylā, ḥammād ibn abī sulaymān, isḥāq, aḥmad, some of dāwūd's companions, and reports from al-zuhrī and ʿaṭāʾ require both rinses in both ghusl and ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن أبي ليلى وحماد بن أبي سليمان): Ibn Abī Laylā, Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān, Isḥāq, Aḥmad, some of Dāwūd's companions, and reports from al-Zuhrī and ʿAṭāʾ require both rinses in both ghusl and ablution.

positions.position: another report from aḥmad makes mouth rinsing recommended but nose rinsing obligatory, a position also held by some of dāwūd's companions
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد وبعض أصحاب داود): Another report from Aḥmad makes mouth rinsing recommended but nose rinsing obligatory, a position also held by some of Dāwūd's companions.

positions.position: a report from ibn ʿumar says prayer was reduced from fifty to five, ghusl from seven washes to one, and washing urine from clothing likewise to one; ibn ʿabd al-barr calls its chain weak and
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): A report from Ibn ʿUmar says prayer was reduced from fifty to five, ghusl from seven washes to one, and washing urine from clothing likewise to one; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr calls its chain weak and notes Shuʿba is not strong.

positions.position: ibn al-qāsim transmits mālik's position that a junub need not work water through the beard
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن القاسم): Ibn al-Qāsim transmits Mālik's position that a junub need not work water through the beard.

positions.position: ashhab transmits the contrary position from mālik: a junub must work water through the beard
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أشهب): Ashhab transmits the contrary position from Mālik: a junub must work water through the beard.

positions.position: ibn ʿabd al-ḥakam prefers working water through the beard because the prophet worked water through his hair; the author reasons that the skin beneath the beard is part of the body to be washed
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عبد الحكم): Ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam prefers working water through the beard because the Prophet worked water through his hair; the author reasons that the skin beneath the beard is part of the body to be washed.

positions.position: the author says lighter ablution rules, such as wiping over footwear, do not transfer to ghusl, which requires water to reach the entire body
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The author says lighter ablution rules, such as wiping over footwear, do not transfer to ghusl, which requires water to reach the entire body.

positions.position: abū ḥanīfa and others require rinsing the mouth and nose in ghusl because both are part of the face; omission requires repeating prayer, though omission in ablution does not
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa and others require rinsing the mouth and nose in ghusl because both are part of the face; omission requires repeating prayer, though omission in ablution does not.

positions.position: anas reports the prophet used one mudd for ablution and one ṣāʿ to five mudds for ghusl; another version gives five makākīk for ghusl and one for ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أنس): Anas reports the Prophet used one mudd for ablution and one ṣāʿ to five mudds for ghusl; another version gives five makākīk for ghusl and one for ablution.

positions.position: those who require the rinses cite this verse and the command to wash faces, adding that the prophet never omitted them in ablution or ghusl
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (من أوجبهما): Those who require the rinses cite this verse and the command to wash faces, adding that the Prophet never omitted them in ablution or ghusl. | mentions 5:6

positions.position: those who distinguish the two say the prophet performed mouth rinsing without commanding it, but both performed and commanded nose rinsing, whose command signifies obligation
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (من فرق بينهما): Those who distinguish the two say the Prophet performed mouth rinsing without commanding it, but both performed and commanded nose rinsing, whose command signifies obligation.

positions.position: the author's scholars require intention for ghusl, as do mālik, al-shāfiʿī, aḥmad, isḥāq, and abū thawr; they also require it for ablution and tayammum
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علماؤنا): The author's scholars require intention for ghusl, as do Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Abū Thawr; they also require it for ablution and tayammum.

positions.position: mālik reports from ʿāʾisha that the prophet bathed from a vessel called a farq; its rāʾ may be vocalized or vowelless
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): Mālik reports from ʿĀʾisha that the Prophet bathed from a vessel called a farq; its rāʾ may be vocalized or vowelless.

positions.position: ibn ʿabbas says a wounded, sore-covered, or smallpox patient in janaba who fears dying from bathing may perform tayammum
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbas says a wounded, sore-covered, or smallpox patient in janaba who fears dying from bathing may perform tayammum.

positions.position: in the cold dhat al-salasil campaign, ʿamr b. al-ʿas feared bathing would kill him, used tayammum, and led dawn prayer while junub; the prophet laughed after hearing his reason
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمرو بن العاص): In the cold Dhat al-Salasil campaign, ʿAmr b. al-ʿAs feared bathing would kill him, used tayammum, and led dawn prayer while junub; the Prophet laughed after hearing his reason.

positions.position: jabir recounts that a companion with a head wound and janaba was told to bathe, died, and the prophet blamed those who failed to tell him to tayammum and bind the wound, wipe over it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (جابر): Jabir recounts that a companion with a head wound and janaba was told to bathe, died, and the Prophet blamed those who failed to tell him to tayammum and bind the wound, wipe over it, and wash the rest.

positions.position: one view limits mulamasa to hand-touch and says a junub person is not covered by the illness clause, so he must bathe or wait for water; it is reported from ʿumar and ibn masʿud
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمر وابن مسعود): One view limits mulamasa to hand-touch and says a junub person is not covered by the illness clause, so he must bathe or wait for water; it is reported from ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿud.

positions.position: an opponent argues by consensus that forced intercourse without pleasure still obligates ghusl, so any touching or kissing should break ablution regardless of desire
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الخصم): An opponent argues by consensus that forced intercourse without pleasure still obligates ghusl, so any touching or kissing should break ablution regardless of desire.

positions.position: scholars agree that only nabidh is even discussed as a substitute drink for water in ablution or ghusl, but the verse's command to tayammum rules that substitution out
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Scholars agree that only nabidh is even discussed as a substitute drink for water in ablution or ghusl, but the verse's command to tayammum rules that substitution out.

positions.position: abu salama reportedly says a junub person who finds water after tayammum remains purified and needs neither ghusl nor ablution until a new occurrence
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو سلمة بن عبد الرحمن): Abu Salama reportedly says a junub person who finds water after tayammum remains purified and needs neither ghusl nor ablution until a new occurrence.

positions.position: the majority hold that a completed prayer after diligent water-search remains valid even if water is then found; some recommend repeating within the time after ablution or ghusl
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور): The majority hold that a completed prayer after diligent water-search remains valid even if water is then found; some recommend repeating within the time after ablution or ghusl.

positions.position: qāḍī ʿiyāḍ knows of no later adherents to the no-ghusl view except al-aʿmash and, afterward, dāwūd al-iṣfahānī
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (القاضي عياض): Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ knows of no later adherents to the no-ghusl view except al-Aʿmash and, afterward, Dāwūd al-Iṣfahānī.

positions.position: ʿumar reportedly made people abandon the report that ghusl is required only when water is emitted
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمر): ʿUmar reportedly made people abandon the report that ghusl is required only when water is emitted.

positions.position: ibn ʿabbās interprets water-from-water as emission during a wet dream; without emission, even a dream of intercourse does not require ghusl, a rule the author says is undisputed
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās interprets water-from-water as emission during a wet dream; without emission, even a dream of intercourse does not require ghusl, a rule the author says is undisputed.

positions.position: abu ʿabd allāh calls ghusl the safer ruling and says the contrary report was included because scholars differed
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عبد الله): Abu ʿAbd Allāh calls ghusl the safer ruling and says the contrary report was included because scholars differed.

positions.position: abū ḥanīfa applies the traveler interpretation: residents generally have water and must bathe, while a traveler without water may use tayammum
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa applies the traveler interpretation: residents generally have water and must bathe, while a traveler without water may use tayammum.

positions.position: ghusl in arabic involves passing the hand with water over what is washed; arabic distinguishes washing cloth from merely pouring or immersing it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Ghusl in Arabic involves passing the hand with water over what is washed; Arabic distinguishes washing cloth from merely pouring or immersing it.

positions.position: the well-known mālikī position and al-muzanī require a junub to rub the body while washing, by analogy with rubbing the face and hands in ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): The well-known Mālikī position and al-Muzanī require a junub to rub the body while washing, by analogy with rubbing the face and hands in ablution.

positions.position: abū al-faraj argues that ghusl linguistically denotes active washing; one who only pours or immerses water is called a pourer or immersed person, not a washer
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو الفرج عمرو بن محمد المالكي): Abū al-Faraj argues that ghusl linguistically denotes active washing; one who only pours or immerses water is called a pourer or immersed person, not a washer.

positions.position: al-aʿmash and dāwūd hold that ghusl is required only of one who has emitted semen; abū ḥayyān says the proofs belong in legal works
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الأعمش وداود): Al-Aʿmash and Dāwūd hold that ghusl is required only of one who has emitted semen; Abū Ḥayyān says the proofs belong in legal works.

positions.position: at dhāt al-salāsil, ʿamr ibn al-ʿāṣ feared bathing would kill him, performed tayammum, and was approved by the prophet; abū ḥayyān cites abū dāwūd and al-dāraquṭnī
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (عمرو بن العاص): At Dhāt al-Salāsil, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ feared bathing would kill him, performed tayammum, and was approved by the Prophet; Abū Ḥayyān cites Abū Dāwūd and al-Dāraquṭnī.

positions.position: the well-known mālikī position and al-muzanī require rubbing the body during ghusl; the majority say immersion or pouring water suffices without rubbing
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (مالك والمزني): The well-known Mālikī position and al-Muzanī require rubbing the body during ghusl; the majority say immersion or pouring water suffices without rubbing.

positions.position: mālik has differing reports on whether the beard must be worked through during ghusl
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (مالك): Mālik has differing reports on whether the beard must be worked through during ghusl.

positions.position: abū ḥanīfa makes mouth rinsing and sniffing obligatory in ghusl but not ablution
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa makes mouth rinsing and sniffing obligatory in ghusl but not ablution.

positions.position: ibn abī laylā, isḥāq, aḥmad, and some of dāwūd's followers require rinsing and sniffing in both ghusl and ablution
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (ابن أبي ليلى وإسحاق وأحمد وبعض أصحاب داود): Ibn Abī Laylā, Isḥāq, Aḥmad, and some of Dāwūd's followers require rinsing and sniffing in both ghusl and ablution.

positions.position: one report from aḥmad and some of dāwūd's followers makes mouth rinsing sunnah and sniffing obligatory
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أحمد وبعض أصحاب داود): One report from Aḥmad and some of Dāwūd's followers makes mouth rinsing sunnah and sniffing obligatory.

positions.position: al-aslaʿ feared that bathing in cold water while in janaba would kill or sicken him; he heated water on stones and washed, after which the verse was revealed
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (الأسلع بن شريك): Al-Aslaʿ feared that bathing in cold water while in janaba would kill or sicken him; he heated water on stones and washed, after which the verse was revealed.

positions.position: aslaʿ ibn sharik reports that on a cold night he feared a bath after becoming junub, so he heated water with hot stones and bathed; revelation then came concerning prayer and the junub traveler
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL, d. 911 (الأسلع بن شريك): Aslaʿ ibn Sharik reports that on a cold night he feared a bath after becoming junub, so he heated water with hot stones and bathed; revelation then came concerning prayer and the junub traveler.

positions.position: saʿid ibn jubayr and mujahid say a sick person who fears harm from bathing for janabah may perform tayammum like a traveler without water
positions.reasons: DURR-FULL, d. 911 (سعيد بن جبير ومجاهد): Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Mujahid say a sick person who fears harm from bathing for janabah may perform tayammum like a traveler without water.

positions.position: al-aslaʿ b. sharīk reports that, fearing illness or death from bathing in icy water after becoming impure while tending the prophet's camel, he told the prophet and the whole verse was revealed
positions.reasons: SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (الأسلع بن شريك): Al-Aslaʿ b. Sharīk reports that, fearing illness or death from bathing in icy water after becoming impure while tending the Prophet's camel, he told the Prophet and the whole verse was revealed.

question: Who are the passers-through excepted here?

positions.position: Travelers lacking water
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): ʿĀbir al-sabīl means a passerby or traveler on the road. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علي وابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد والحكم): ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, Mujāhid, and al-Ḥakam interpret the exception as referring to a traveler. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): The exception describes a junub traveler passing through, and the reference to travel reflects the usual lack of water on a journey. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The traveler is called a passer of the road because he is on the road, as in the expression son of the road. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): Alternatively, عابري describes جنبا, with إلا meaning غير: the prohibition concerns resident, unexcused people in janāba; this is clear if عبور means travel. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali says the exception concerns a traveler who becomes sexually impure, lacks water, performs tayammum, and prays until water becomes available. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas identifies the exception as a traveler who has no water and therefore performs tayammum and prays. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujahid glosses the exception as travelers who cannot find water. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Among scholars who use legal implications, the unqualified traveler exception is further limited by “if you find no water”; the general prohibition on junub people is otherwise narrowed by the later illness-or-travel condition. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): If Muslims already understood that prayer may occur without purification, the traveler exception awaits clarification and the following conditions clarify it; otherwise, those conditions introduce tayammum rules anew. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Ali, İbn Abbas, İbn Cübeyr, Mücâhid, Ebû Hanîfe): Ali, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and Abu Hanifa understand passers as travelers, the translation's choice; travel can make water unavailable or too necessary to use, so tayammum is allowed for a junub traveler. positions.position: People crossing a mosque
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (عبد الله وسعيد بن المسيب والضحاك وعكرمة والحسن): Another interpretation is do not approach mosques for prayer or otherwise; the exception for passing supports this because crossing is physical movement through a place. TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Abir means crossing from one side of a river or road to the other. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The verb ʿabara describes crossing a road or river from one side to the other. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The author answers the comparison with minor impurity by saying it occurs often and cleansing it would cause hardship; the verse's crossing exception suffices. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): ʿĀbir means crossing or passing through; the cited verse uses عبر for traversing the heat of midday. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī understands the passer as someone who walks through a mosque without staying there. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): On the reading of prayer as the mosque, al-Zamakhsharī takes the exception to permit only passing through on a route to water, where water is in the mosque, or after a wet dream there. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (علي وابن عباس وابن جبير ومجاهد والحكم): These authorities identify the passer as a traveler: a junub may not approach prayer until washing, except a traveler may use tayammum. Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, Mālik, al-Thawrī, and others bar even mosque passage. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): One parse makes عابري a circumstantial exception governed by the prohibition: do not approach in janāba except while traveling or crossing a mosque, depending on the interpretation. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhshari takes the exception as a circumstantial phrase from the addressees generally, with travel as an additional excuse and crossing the path as its expression. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): One interpretation supplies an omitted مضاف: ‘the places of prayer,’ meaning mosques; the exception for crossing a path supports this in one reading. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas interprets the exception as allowing a junub person to pass through a mosque without sitting; Ibn Kathir lists many authorities who agree, including Ibn Masud, Anas, Abu Ubayda, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, Qatada, and others. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir explains an abir al-sabil as one who passes and crosses through; Arabic uses the same root for crossing a road or river and calls a camel able to cross journeys abir asfar. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud interprets the exception as passing through the mosque; he elsewhere permits a junub person to cross it in transit. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): On the mosque interpretation of prayer, crossing through a mosque is allowed for a junub person; al-Shafi'i holds this, while the well-known Hanafi position forbids mosque entry absolutely. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (من حمل الصلاة على مواضعها): One parsing takes prayer as its locations and crossing as passing through them, so the later condition states a distinct rule. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The recommended pause after “until you wash” and the spatial language of approaching, crossing, and travel support that interpretation. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الكثير): Many commentators take the passage otherwise than the spatial interpretation of prayer and crossing. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): In Arabic, a traveler while on a journey is an “ʿābir al-sabīl,” from crossing or passing through a river or road. TABATABAI, d. 1402 (author): Al-ṣalāt here means the mosque, because the exception for passers-through fits a rule about a junub entering the mosque. STUDYQURAN (author): The exception covers junub travelers seeking temporary shelter in a mosque and Companions whose adjacent homes required crossing the Prophet’s mosque to leave. question: What illness permits tayammum?

positions.position: Illness named as a qualifying state
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Coming from the ghait is a euphemism for relieving oneself; or can mean and, because illness and travel permit tayammum while using the toilet requires purification. | mentions 37:147 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): A second report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the sick person was granted permission to use clean earth for tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (داود): Dawud reads the term sick literally: anyone who can be called ill may use tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو يوسف وزفر): Abu Yusuf and Zufar prohibit tayammum for residents, whether the reason is illness or fear that prayer time will end. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik treats illness and travel as the usual cases where water is absent: residents and healthy people may analogically use tayammum if water is unavailable, obstructed, or time would pass. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi prefers aw in its ordinary sense, with ellipsis: illness preventing water use, or travel with no water and a need for it. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The illness may make water use dangerous or prevent reaching it; in either case, the person is treated as lacking water. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): The dry-ablution command covers the sick, travelers, people with minor impurity, and those in major impurity; it applies when each lacks usable water for the relevant reason. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): Not finding water normally means searching without reaching it; for the sick, existing water that cannot be used counts legally as absent. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī's stated position disallows tayammum for that fear, though his correct view is reported to permit it when long illness is feared. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī explains that illness and travel are named first because they commonly create need for the concession, then the rule extends to anyone obliged to purify but lacking water through an enemy, beast, missing drawing tool, isolation, or similar cause. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (بعض العلماء): Some scholars permit tayammum for illness generally, relying on the verse’s broad wording. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): The verse guards prayer from impairment by drunkenness, junub status, or minor impurity, while making a merciful tayammum exception for illness or lack of water. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujahid says a sick person who becomes junub and fears for his life receives the same tayammum concession as a traveler without water. SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (مجاهد): Mujāhid says the clause about illness was revealed for an Anṣārī who could not rise to wash and had no servant to bring water, so he told the Prophet. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Jurists permit dry ablution in the first two illness categories but not the third, where only a blemish or defect is feared. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The wording's general expression followed by detail is more eloquent and emphatic than explicitly listing travelers and patients lacking water, while accommodating different levels of understanding. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Illness means any condition that prevents water use, whether because water cannot be reached or cannot safely be used. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (قيل): Travel is mentioned to connect illness with travel and equate them through inability to use water, even when water is present. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعضهم): A proposal reorders the verse: prohibit prayer in intoxication, janaba, or after either event, then command tayammum for illness or travel; al-Alusi objects that it splits condition and result without rationale. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Al-Alusi prefers the apparent order: waterlessness can mean inability to use water and govern all cases, or retain its literal sense without attaching it to illness and travel. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Illness and travel need not be restricted to people already in minor or major impurity: the verse explains the switch from water purification to tayammum. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): People outside illness and travel illustrate that inability to use water for other reasons also licenses tayammum; the ritual event itself is not the cause. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (قيل): One explanation says water absence also conditions illness and travel, but need not be repeated because major impurity is already clear there and minor impurity follows by textual implication. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (مالك): In the Baghdadi transmission, a patient unable to use water may perform multiple prayers with one tayammum until a nullifier; this also applies to missed prayers, and no Malik report addresses a junub person who then loses wudu. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The water condition does not restrict the sick person's tayammum, because the meaning of illness already indicates the concession. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The sick person is not merely someone chronically bedridden, since someone can usually bring water to such a person. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 (author): When water is unavailable or cannot be used due to illness, tayammum replaces both the full bath after intercourse and the partial pre-prayer ablution. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Illness or travel alone does not grant the tayammum dispensation; water must also be unavailable or unusable. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Because residents and healthy people may also perform tayammum when water is absent, the commentary asks why illness and travel are singled out. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Another answer is that illness and travel are singled out because water is more likely to be absent or unusable then. STUDYQURAN (author): Clean earth substitutes for water when illness prevents seeking or safely using water, or on a journey where water is unavailable. | mentions 5:6 STUDYQURAN (legal schools): Schools differ on water-search requirements, illness threshold, whether tayammum removes impurity or temporarily permits prayer, and whether prayer must be repeated if water is found before prayer time ends. positions.position: Water-use harm or delayed recovery qualifies
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (ابن عباس وابن مسعود والسدي والضحاك ومجاهد وقتادة): One view permits tayammum for wounds, fractures, and sores when the person fears harm from water. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Within the Maliki school, even less severe illness permits tayammum when water risks causing, worsening, or prolonging illness; Ibn ʿAtiyya says this is what he recalls as consensus. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Al-Baji reports that Qadi Abu al-Hasan and Abu Hanifa permit tayammum for a healthy person fearing a cold or fever, and for a patient fearing worsening illness. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabi argues that worsening illness is uncertain, so it cannot justify abandoning the certain duty to use water. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAtiyya calls Dawud's view an outlier; scholars mean illness harmed by water, such as smallpox or fever, as in Ibn ʿAbbas's report. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (العلماء): Other jurists restrict illness to conditions such as smallpox, measles, or dangerous ailments where water may harm; they agree tayammum is allowed when harm is feared. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو حنيفة ومالك): Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik permit tayammum when one fears illness will begin or worsen, or recovery will be delayed. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Illness permits tayammum when using water risks losing or damaging a limb, or prolonging recovery. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says the sick allowed tayammum include the broken and wounded; when junub, they should not wash a wound if doing so risks harm. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud says the patient allowed dry ablution includes a person with a fracture or wound; if he becomes junub, he should not wash an injury when that risks harm. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas, in a report raised to the Prophet, says a person with a wound, ulcers, or smallpox who fears washing while junub may use dry ablution. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The verse's unrestricted wording appears to allow every sick person dry ablution, but other verses exclude those whose illness will not worsen; legal works detail the rule. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Not finding water can figuratively mean that water exists but cannot be used because of need, fear, or harm; such circumstances are more common for travelers and the sick.

positions.position: Fear of death or loss of limb
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (القاضي أبو يعلى): Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā says illness allows tayammum when using water would cause harm, whether or not death is feared; travel allows it with no water on short or long journeys. Lack of water is not required for the ill, but harm is; it is required for travelers, while travel itself is not a condition because water is commonly absent on journeys. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الحسن وعطاء): Severe illness that risks death from water or loss of a limb permits tayammum by consensus; al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ dissent, but al-Qurtubi rejects their view by the no-hardship and no-self-killing verses. | mentions 22:78, 4:29 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi answers that if fear of death from cold permits tayammum, fear of illness should also suffice, since both illness and death are harms. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو نصر عبد الرحيم القشيري): Al-Qushayri gives the sound Shafiʿi position: fear of death or losing a limb permits tayammum, and the sound view also permits it to avoid prolonged illness. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Since the Prophet allowed travelling ʿAmr to use tayammum when bathing risked death, a sick person is even more entitled to it. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): A report raised to the Prophet applies the tayammum concession to a person with war wounds, sores, or smallpox who fears bathing would kill him. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): The verse gives three illness levels: water would cause death; it would cause severe pain, worsen or prolong illness; or it would leave only a feared blemish or bodily defect. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The established Hanafi rule permits dry ablution when using water is expected to worsen illness, whether worsening comes from movement or water itself; fear of death is not required. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (جمهور العلماء): All other jurists reject Umar and Ibn Masud's restriction; the majority allow tayammum for lack of water or fear that washing will cause death, illness, or worsening, even a cold or fever. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi permits tayammum only for lack of water or fear of death, reasoning that worsening illness is uncertain; Ibn Ashur replies that both outcomes are uncertain and God imposes no hardship.

positions.position: Inability to obtain or handle water
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): The condition covers sick people and travelers: a traveler lacks water, while a sick person may have no one to wash him or fear harm from water. TABRISI, d. 548 (الحسن وابن زيد): Another view permits it when illness makes someone unable to handle water and no one can bring it; Hasan did not allow an injured person to use tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Illness counts when no one can hand over water or its use is feared harmful; a healthy resident may also lack usable water through widespread exorbitant prices, imprisonment, or restraint. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن زيد): Ibn Zayd says a sick person without anyone to bring water, who cannot reach it and has no helper, may perform tayammum and pray.

positions.position: Any illness qualifies
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (داود): Dāwūd applies the general wording of illness without limits on severity or duration and allows tayammum to anyone who fits the name sick.

question: What journeys qualify for tayammum?

positions.position: Travel when water is unavailable
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (فرقة): Another group disallows tayammum during sinful travel; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also judges this weak. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (author): A traveler may lack water because none exists, searching risks missing companions, baggage is endangered, or predators or other harm threaten. TABRISI, d. 548 (علي وابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد): One interpretation forbids prayer in janaba except for travelers, who may pray using tayammum even though it does not remove janaba. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أصحاب الشافعي): They argue the travel and water ruling follows as a separate rule: readers prefer pausing at ‘until you wash,’ so the earlier exception should not depend on the later verse’s condition. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): A traveler who lacks water must use tayammum whether the journey is long or short. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Scholars agree tayammum is allowed while travelling, but disagree about residence: Malik, his followers, Abu Hanifa, and Muhammad allow it there too. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar reportedly would not leave his travel route to seek water even when it lay two bowshots away; Ishaq says one need search only where one is. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): A traveler may tayammum if water is entirely or partly unavailable, or seeking it risks losing companions or baggage, encountering thieves or beasts, missing prayer time, or causing thirst to oneself or another; cooking necessary food also counts. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو سعيد الخدري): In the report of Abu Said, two travelers pray after tayammum; the Prophet says the one who does not repeat followed the Sunna and the one who repeats earns double reward. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو داود): Abu Dawud transmits the two-traveler report and notes that the Abu Said link is not preserved in other narrations; al-Daraqutni's version specifies finding water within the prayer time. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (قتادة): Asked about travel tayammum, Qatada reports Ibn Umar’s elbow limit; al-Hasan and Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i also held it. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The traveler is excused when water is unavailable. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The exception attaches to “while junub,” exempting travel when water is unavailable and tayammum is used, as the following clause indicates. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa allows tayammum for someone who leaves town without intending travel if water is a mile away; another view sets the distance where people's voices cannot be heard. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Travel permits tayammum whether the journey is long or short. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (عمار بن ياسر): Ammar ibn Yasir reports that after he became junub while traveling and rolled in dust, the Prophet taught him that tayammum requires only striking the earth and wiping the face and palms. SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (علي): ʿAlī says the clause about being ritually impure except when passing through concerns a traveler who became impure, performed dry ablution, and prayed. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): A traveler excused by travel may pray using dry ablution while junub; the prohibition lasts until washing. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الهداية): Al-Hidaya allows tayammum for someone without water who is traveling or at least a mile outside town. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Abirin sabil means people traveling on the road or in a state of travel; the exception concerns tayammum. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): The failure to find water is attached to the conditional clause and limits the traveler, one coming from the privy, and one touching women. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Although the verse later explicitly refers to travelers, this interpretation says the phrase is repeated because water is less available or more needed during travel. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Scholars agree tayammum is permissible during travel when water is absent or an obstacle prevents its use. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): The commentary reads this verse as stating the tayammum substitute during travel and 5:6 as stating it for residents. | mentions 5:6 STUDYQURAN (the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah): The verse reportedly followed ʿĀʾishah losing a necklace while traveling with the Prophet. The group camped to search, lacked water, complained they could not wash, and the verse came at dawn prayer. MAJAZ (source note MAJAZ:v1p128/r1) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58/r5) supports this position.

positions.position: Only a qualifying journey
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الشافعي وقوم): Al-Shāfiʿī reports a view that tayammum is allowed only on travel that permits shortening prayer; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): When water is unavailable, tayammum is allowed on a journey of any length under Malik and most scholars; requiring a prayer-shortening or devotional journey is weak.

positions.position: Any journey, short or long
positions.reasons: BURSEVI, d. 1127 (أبو حنيفة): Travel, short or long, is cited to establish the ruling and its procedure; the rule also applies wherever water cannot be used, and Abu Hanifa permits tayammum for janabah in town without hot water.

question: What does al-ghāʾiṭ mean?

positions.position: ghait means a low place where people relieved themselves out of sight; its name became a euphemism for the act or result. another account says it was named for what people discarded there; murajj defines
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Ghait means a low place where people relieved themselves out of sight; its name became a euphemism for the act or result. positions.position: al-ghāʾiṭ literally means low, level ground; the place is used euphemistically for the act of excretion, like other container or vehicle terms used for their contents

positions.position: al-ghāʾiṭ originally means a low, concealing place; people sought one to relieve themselves out of sight, and the bodily event later took the place’s name. its plural is ghīṭān

question: What does touching women mean?

positions.position: Both bodily contact and intercourse
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (ابن عباس): When Arabs and non-Arabs disagreed whether it meant intercourse or touching, Ibn Abbas said the non-Arabs were right: it means intercourse, called touch because it leads to intercourse. TABRISI, d. 548 (علي وابن عباس ومجاهد والسدي وقتادة): One interpretation takes touching women to mean intercourse; Abu Hanifa and al-Jubbaʾi adopt it. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (علي، ابن عباس، الحسن، مجاهد، قتادة): One legal interpretation takes touching women to mean sexual intercourse. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أنصار قول الجماع): Supporters of the intercourse interpretation cite Qur’anic euphemisms for intercourse at 2:37 and 58:3; Ibn ʿAbbās says God is modest and noble, veiling the meaning with ‘touching.’ | mentions 2:37, 58:3 RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أنصار قول الجماع): They also argue that ‘coming from the place of need’ already covers minor impurity; if touching women also meant minor impurity, the verse would omit major impurity, so it must mean intercourse. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The three reported meanings are intercourse, physical contact, or a word covering both; most readers treat the two readings as equivalent in sense. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (محمد بن يزيد): Muhammad b. Yazid says lamastum more naturally means kissing or the like, since each party acts; lamistum means intercourse or touching, where the woman does not act. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن العربي): Ibn al-ʿArabi says the verse assigns three clauses to three rulings: janaba, minor impurity, and touch or kissing; treating touch as intercourse would repeat the meaning. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Although the reciprocal form mulamasa is said to require two actors, al-Qurtubi answers that both parties can be described as toucher and touched; Arabic also uses reciprocal verbs for one actor. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Masḥ can mean intercourse, cutting with a sword, a camel's day's travel, a woman without buttocks, or a touch of beauty; here it means dragging the hand across the object. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (علي وابن عباس): Ali and Ibn ʿAbbās explain touching women here as sexual intercourse. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The long-alif form can correspond to the simple verb, like جاوزت الشيء وجزته; its form does not distinguish active from passive though the meaning can, and al-Shāfiʿī applies it to both toucher and touched in his stronger view. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (غير مسمى): One interpretation makes فاعل equivalent to a simple verb; another says لمس means intercourse while لامس denotes touching short of intercourse. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عمر وعبيدة وأبو عثمان النهدي وأبو عبيدة وعامر الشعبي وثابت بن الحجاج وإبراهيم النخعي وزيد بن أسلم): Ibn Abi Hatim transmits the interpretation that touch means less than intercourse from these authorities as well. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ناصر هذه المقالة): Advocates of the physical-touch reading cite Quran 6:7, prophetic usage toward Ma‘iz, the hadith about the hand’s zina, Aisha’s report of the Prophet kissing and touching his wives, and the Sahihayn prohibition of touch-sale; they say Arabic uses the word for both touch and intercourse. | mentions 6:7 IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس وعلي وأبي بن كعب ومجاهد وطاوس والحسن وعبيد بن عمير وسعيد بن جبير والشعبي وقتادة ومقاتل بن حيان): One interpretation takes touching women as a euphemism for intercourse, held by these authorities; Quranic uses of touching in divorce contexts support that sense. | mentions 2:237, 33:49 BURHAN, d. 794 (author): The Qur'an euphemizes intercourse with terms for touching, intimacy, marital union, entry, and covering, drawing on bodily contact and clothing or cultivation metaphors. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī allows lamastum to mean literal skin contact, intercourse caused by contact, or a particular kind of touching; intercourse can be named by its cause or the whole by a part. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (علي بن أبي طالب): Ali says “touching women” means sexual intercourse, expressed euphemistically by God. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas glosses touching women as sexual intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): In a discussion, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Ata, and the non-Arab clients argued for hand-touch, while Ubayd ibn Umayr and the Arabs argued for intercourse; Ibn Abbas judged the Arabs right, since touch-related terms can euphemize intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas tells Nafi ibn al-Azraq that the verse means intercourse, though Hudhayl uses the word for hand-touch; he cites Labid and al-Aʿsha's poems as evidence for that Arabic usage. ITQAN, d. 911 (author): The reported difference over whether لامستم means intercourse or touching by hand is no disagreement: intercourse fits لامستم, and hand-touch fits لمستم. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (author): Touching women here means having intercourse with them. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): “Touching women” euphemistically means intercourse, indicating major impurity, while the preceding clause indicates minor impurity. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (ابن مسعود والنخعي والشعبي): Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Shaʿbi interpret the phrase as skin touching short of intercourse. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعضهم): Others prefer interpreting both readings as intercourse, privileging figurative usage and reconciling the readings; this matches the Hanafi position. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Touch literally means bodily contact, and metaphorically can mean seeking or finding, descending, or sexual intercourse; the cited poem witnesses the sense of descending, while 2:237 uses it for intercourse. | mentions 72:8, 2:237 KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): Lems and mulamasa literally mean touching with a hand or part of the body, while figuratively they mean sexual intercourse. positions.position: Sexual intercourse
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Al-Tabrisi prefers intercourse: the verse already addresses the junub when water is present and must state the junub’s rule when absent as well as the rule for one who relieved himself. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (ابن مسعود وابن عمر والشعبي والنخعي والشافعي): Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, and al-Shāfiʿī understand the phrase as skin contact, with or without intercourse. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (ابن عباس): Ibn ʿAbbās explains that God is modest and noble and uses euphemism, calling sexual intimacy ‘touching.’ QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Against the claim that Ibn ʿAbbas interpreted mulamasa as intercourse, al-Qurtubi notes that ʿUmar, his son, and Ibn Masʿud opposed it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): In the cited poetic usage, junub means a stranger; janāba also denotes a man's intercourse with a woman. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Alternatively, the phrase means sexual intercourse; lamasa is less commonly used as a euphemism for intercourse than mulāmasa. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (علي وابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة): ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and Qatāda interpret the phrase as intercourse, in which case a junub may use tayammum. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزمخشري): Al-Zamakhsharī takes لمس النساء as intercourse resulting in janāba, following the Ḥanafī school, and reports no other school's view. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس): Ibn Kathir says Ibn Abbas’s intercourse interpretation is soundly transmitted through multiple routes. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas explains lamastum as intercourse, saying that God may use whatever euphemism He wills; Sa‘id ibn Jubayr reports Ibn Abbas’s response to the disagreement between Arab and non-Arab groups. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (أبو عبيدة): Abu Ubayda says the contact means what is short of intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (الشعبي): Al-Shabi says the contact means what is short of intercourse. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (الحسن): Al-Hasan interprets the contact as sexual intercourse. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (علي وابن عباس والحسن): ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan are cited for the intercourse reading, which indicates major impurity. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (بعض المحققين): Some investigators say mutual bodily contact by any body part is the literal meaning, which includes intercourse; it is metaphor only when intercourse alone is intended. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Ibn Ashur prefers the euphemistic sense of intercourse: the list gathers common causes of minor and major purification, and the concession context calls for explicit mention rather than relying on implication. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 (author): Junub describes the state after sexual intercourse; from janaba, “to make remote,” it denotes distance from prayer due to immersion in sexual passion. positions.position: A touch related sense
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Touching and mutual touch have the same meaning, since one cannot touch a woman without her touching him. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي ومحمد بن عبد الحكم): Al-Shafiʿi and Muhammad b. ʿAbd al-Hakam count anything from either outlet, even if unusual, and include touching. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): Junub may derive from distance, since one is apart from purity, or from the side, since one lies with or touches another by his side. SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): جنب derives from جنابة, ‘distance’; a person is so called either for being distant from purity or for lying beside and touching another. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): The phrase is recited in two forms: lamastum and lamastum (with the long vowel). Exegetes and jurists differ over its meaning. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): The cited wording about touching women, with references to 4:43 and 5:6, is another example attached to the preceding discussion of literal and figurative usage. | mentions 4:43, 5:6 DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud also glosses touching women as ghamz, pressing or squeezing. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Variants such as yathurna/yattahharna and lamastum/lamastum increase the possible meanings of a verse. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (حمزة والكسائي وخلف): Most readers recite lāmastum with an alif; Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, and Khalaf recite lamastum without one. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (author): After intending tayammum, one touches clean soil, clay, sand, or stone with the palms, wipes the face, touches again, then wipes arms to the elbows. QIRAAT-ER (Ḥamza and Kisāʾī): Ḥamza and Kisāʾī read Form I lamasa instead of Form III lāmasa, removing the reciprocal morpheme and indicating one-sided touching. STUDYQURAN (legal scholars): Legal scholars hold that major ritual impurity also prohibits touching or reciting the Quran.

positions.position: Bodily touch short of intercourse
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود والشعبي وعطاء): Another interpretation takes it as touching a woman by hand or otherwise; al-Shafiʿi adopts this view. TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Touch first referred to the hand and then broadened beyond literal contact; iltamas means to seek. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (ابن مسعود، ابن عمر، الشعبي، عبيدة، عطاء، ابن سيرين، النخعي، النهدي، الحكم، حماد): Another legal interpretation takes the phrase as touching a woman with the hand. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (أبو علي): Abū ʿAlī says touch can mean contact by hand but is extended to other kinds of contact; 72:8 uses “we touched the heaven” for attempting to reach its secrets. | mentions 72:8 IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (أبو علي): The wording “they touched it with their hands” in 6:7 specifies hands to distinguish literal touching from the extended sense; likewise “sons from your loins” in 4:23 distinguishes biological sons from merely named sons. | mentions 6:7, 4:23 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The Maliki nullifiers fall into three kinds; Hanafis count impure bodily emissions regardless of outlet but exclude touching. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): When ʿUrwa asked which wife the Prophet kissed, ʿAisha laughed, leaving open that she herself was the one. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الدارقطني): The kiss report used by Abu Hanifa is mursal: Daraqutni notes that Habib b. Abi Thabit did not hear from ʿUrwa, as Yahya b. Saʿid says Sufyan al-Thawri maintained. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): Aisha reports that while searching for the Prophet at night in the mosque, her hand touched the soles of his feet as he prayed in prostration. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Scholars agree that tayammum does not remove major or minor ritual impurity; finding water restores the person to the prior state, based on the Prophet's instruction to Abu Dharr to let water touch his skin. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو عمر): Abū ʿUmar says no regional jurists adopted the hand-touch view, citing reports about tayammum for a junub from ʿAmmār, Abū Dharr, and ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): An unattributed poem uses ‘I touched the palm of his hand’ to illustrate the physical-touch sense of the verb. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو ذر): The Prophet says clean earth purifies a Muslim even after ten years without water; once water is available, the person should let it touch the skin. Al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih, and Ibn Hibban authenticates it. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (حماد): Hammad says anything touched by one's hands counts as saʿid, even dust from a saddle pad, and may be used for tayammum. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (أبو عثمان): Abu Uthman interprets the contact as touching by hand. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الجلال المحلي والكمال ابن أبي شريف): Al-Jalal al-Mahalli calls touching by hand literal; Ibn Abi Sharif says this exemplifies one kind of touch rather than defining the full literal meaning. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Touching earth with the hands evokes purification because earth is the source of water and is also used to clean vessels, garments, bodies, and through istijmar; it reminds the waterless person to seek water once able. ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 (author): Tayammum is performed by touching earth or a dust-bearing substance with the palms, then lightly wiping the face and hands. QIRAAT-ER (Shāfiʿī): The Shāfiʿī view takes Form I as one-sided touching, so any skin contact breaks wuḍūʾ.

question: When does contact with a woman invalidate ablution?

positions.position: Any direct bodily contact invalidates ablution
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الجمهور): The majority requires wiping the whole face within its known ablution boundaries, carefully ensuring no part is left untouched. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-ghaʾit covers minor ablution nullifiers; the strongest Maliki classification groups them as loss of reason, customary discharge, and touching. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa takes mulamasa to mean intercourse alone: a junub person may tayammum, but hand-touch and a pleasurable kiss do not invalidate ablution. Ziyad says touching through a thick garment has no effect, but touching through a thin one requires ablution. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi calls the Maliki position strongest: touch short of intercourse invalidates ablution, as reported from ʿUmar, his son, and Ibn Masʿud and held by most jurists. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi's view that uncovered skin-contact with a woman breaks ablution follows the apparent wording, whether he touches her or she touches him. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Qurtubi says it is good precaution to perform ablution after touching a woman's hair. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The claim that the mere act of touching invalidates ablution would also make a man lose ablution by slapping his wife to discipline her, an implication Qurtubi says no one accepts. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): One Shafi'i opinion says touching even a little girl invalidates ablution based on the word “women”; Qurtubi rejects it, likening a child's touch to touching a wall. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الأوزاعي): Al-Awza'i says he would advise a man who asks about kissing his wife to renew ablution, but would not blame him if he did not. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The phrase may mean skin touching skin; al-Shāfiʿī uses it as evidence that touching women invalidates ablution. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (آخرون): Other interpreters take the phrase to mean any bodily touching, requiring wudu when any part of a man’s body touches a woman’s body directly. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عبد الله بن مسعود): Ibn Masud says touching means contact short of intercourse; he also reports that a kiss counts as touch and requires wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar performed wudu after kissing a woman and considered the kiss part of al-limas; Ibn Kathir also cites Ibn Umar’s statement that kissing or touching one’s wife by hand requires wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عمر بن الخطاب): Al-Daraqutni transmits from Umar a report similar to requiring wudu after touch; another report says Umar kissed his wife and prayed without wudu, so Ibn Kathir says the former, if sound, may indicate recommendation. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (الشافعي وأصحابه ومالك وأحمد بن حنبل): Requiring wudu after physical touch is the position of al-Shafi‘i and his followers, Malik, and the well-known position from Ahmad. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (معاذ): In a report from Muadh, a man says he met a woman and did everything short of intercourse; Quran 11:114 was revealed, and the Prophet ordered him to perform wudu and pray, saying the ruling applies to all believers. Al-Tirmidhi calls the report disconnected and al-Nasa’i transmits it as mursal. | mentions 11:114 IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن جرير): Ibn Jarir prefers intercourse as the meaning, citing a report that the Prophet kissed one of his wives and then prayed without renewing wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عائشة): Aisha reports that the Prophet kissed one of his wives, then went out to pray without renewing wudu; when asked who the wife was, she smiled. Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah transmit it. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عائشة): Aisha reports that the Prophet kissed her after wudu and did not repeat it; a route through Ibrahim al-Taymi is also transmitted, but Abu Dawud and al-Nasa’i say Ibrahim did not hear from her. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أم سلمة): Umm Salama reports that the Prophet kissed her while fasting, did not break his fast, and did not renew wudu. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (زينب السهمية): Zaynab al-Sahmiyya reports that the Prophet would kiss and then pray without performing wudu; Ahmad also transmits a route through Aisha. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن مسعود): Ibn Masud explains touching women as contact short of intercourse, including kissing, and says it requires ablution. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar used to perform ablution after kissing a woman, saying that a kiss is touching. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar says kissing one's wife or touching her by hand is contact that requires ablution. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (عمر): Umar says kissing is a form of touching and requires ablution. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (محمد بن سيرين): Muhammad ibn Sirin says he was told Ibn Umar performed ablution after touching his private part; he took this and Ubayda's gesture to be the same interpretation. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (أبو ذر): Abu Dharr reports the Prophet saying pure earth serves as a Muslim's ablution for up to ten years without water; when water is found, it should touch the skin. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي والزهري والأوزاعي): Al-Shafiʿi infers that touching a woman invalidates ablution; al-Zuhri and al-Awzaʿi agree. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi reads the phrase literally and makes a man's touching a woman's body with his hand invalidate wudu; Ibn Ashur calls this an implausible reading.
