positions.position: Ordinary touch does not invalidate ablution
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وقتادة وأبو حنيفة): Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Qatāda, and Abū Ḥanīfa take touching women to mean intercourse, since touching by hand does not invalidate ablution. RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (أهل الظاهر): The literalists hold that only the person who touches a woman loses ablution; the person touched does not. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik says intercourse calls for tayammum; hand-touch calls for ablution if pleasure is felt, while touch without desire does not, a view also held by Ahmad and Ishaq. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الأوزاعي): Al-Awzaʿi says hand-touch invalidates ablution but other bodily contact does not, citing the verse about touching with their hands. | mentions 6:7 QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): In al-Shafiʿi's view, touching hair, teeth, or nails does not break ablution; precaution favors ablution after touching hair. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Touching through clothing does not break ablution even with pleasure; direct skin contact counts whether deliberate or forgetful and whether the unrelated woman is alive or dead. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi has two views on touching a young girl, elderly woman, or unmarriageable female: it breaks ablution under the verse's general wording, or does not because desire is irrelevant to them. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (المروزي): Al-Marwazi prefers the unrestricted Shafiʿi view because the verse does not condition touch on desire, as also reflected by Companions and most Successors. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi rejects the objection that the Prophet could not touch ʿAisha through clothing: the report expressly describes him as touching her, and the Sunnah specifies that touch without desire or intent does not invalidate ablution. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The reports show that direct touch does not invalidate ablution for every person who touches; Qurtubi's rule distinguishes touch according to pleasure. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو ثور): Abu Thawr holds that kissing, intimate contact, or touching one's wife does not require ablution; Qurtubi associates this with the Hanafi school. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (أبو حنيفة): Abū Ḥanīfa reads the phrase as intercourse, not hand-touch; even a kiss with desire does not invalidate ablution in his school. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): The report does not establish wudu for touching because Abu Layla did not meet Muadh, leaving a gap in the chain. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa holds that touching does not invalidate ablution, even with desire; another qualification says it does if erection occurs. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi differed over touching close relatives or a young unrelated woman; his sounder view is that it does not invalidate ablution, like touching teeth, nails, or hair. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi does not invalidate the touched person's ablution when their private part is touched, since that person did not touch a locus of pleasure. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The Hanafi view, followed by Elmalılı, excludes mere skin contact from the meaning; touching a woman's body alone does not invalidate ablution. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Mâlik, Ahmed, İshak): Malik, Ahmad, and Ishaq hold that touching with sexual pleasure invalidates ablution, while touching without that aim does not. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Evzâî): Al-Awza'i holds that touching with the hand invalidates ablution, but touching with another part of the body does not. KURANYOLU-TEFSIR (Şevkânî): Al-Shawkani says the word fits both senses, so neither can determine a ruling; Prophetic and Companion practice shows skin contact alone does not invalidate ablution and intercourse is meant. The commentary endorses this.

positions.position: Touch with desire or intent for pleasure
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عبد الملك بن الماجشون): Ibn al-Majishun requires ablution for intentionally touching one's wife by hand for play, whether or not pleasure follows. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (القاضي أبو الوليد الباجي): Al-Baji clarifies the Maliki rule: intending pleasure by touching requires ablution whether pleasure actually occurs or not. Aḥmad and Isḥāq agree on the desire distinction. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (مالك والليث بن سعد وأحمد): Malik, al-Layth, and one report from Ahmad say touching invalidates ablution only when accompanied by desire. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الشافعي): In al-Shafiʿi's stronger view, the person touched also loses ablution because both participants share the possibility of pleasure, as in intercourse. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (مالك): Malik treats the phrase as both literal and euphemistic but invalidates wudu for literal touch only with pleasure or intent to take pleasure; Ibn Ashur attributes this to early reports, not the verse's intended sense. question: When is water legally unavailable?

positions.position: Water is physically absent
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الحسن وعطاء): Al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ say the explicit condition of finding no water bars everyone from tayammum when water is available; Abu ʿUmar says this would be sound without the majority view and transmitted reports. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (بعض من ألف في أحكام القرآن): A writer on Quranic rulings argues that because “water” is indefinite, tayammum is forbidden whenever any amount of water exists, mixed with other matter or alone. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi argues that “not finding water” means one must first seek it, and tayammum is a necessity purification like that of a woman with continuous bleeding. BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): “Finding no water” includes being unable to use it, since what one is barred from using counts as unavailable. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عمران بن حصين): In a report in both Sahih collections, the Prophet asks a Muslim who sat apart from the prayer group why he did not pray; the man says he is junub and has no water, and the Prophet tells him that clean earth suffices. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم): Ammar reports that the Prophet camped at Awlat al-Jaysh with Aisha; after her Dhafar-bead necklace was lost and water was unavailable until dawn, God granted tayammum. The Muslims struck earth without taking up dust and wiped faces and hands to shoulders and armpits. BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 (author): Not finding water includes either its absence or inability to use it. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (حذيفة): Hudhayfa reports the Prophet saying that earth was made a purifying substance for the community when water is unavailable. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): Naming the events before waterlessness signals that lack of water licenses relief only after purification becomes obligatory. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (النبي): People in sandy country with no water for a month or two, including people in janaba, menstruation, and postpartum impurity, are told by the Prophet to use their land. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p318/r6) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p318/r7) supports this position. JISHUMI (source note JISHUMI:v2p1567/r19) supports this position. KASHSHAF-FULL (source note KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p547/r6) supports this position.

question: Must one search for water before tayammum?

positions.position: A search is required
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī requires a fresh search for water when each prayer time begins after a person has prayed using tayammum, since not finding it implies prior searching. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik's apparent position, shared by al-Shafi'i, makes searching for water a condition for valid tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa and Qadi Abu Muhammad ibn Nasr hold that searching for water is not a condition of valid tayammum. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi prefers requiring a search: the verse's “not finding water” presupposes looking, and a substitute is usable only when inability to obtain the original is certain. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa, his two companions, and al-Muzani allow tayammum before the prayer time because searching for water is not a condition, analogizing to voluntary prayer. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو الفرج): Abu al-Faraj permits making up multiple missed prayers with one tayammum; this assumes water-search is not a condition, which Qurtubi rejects. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik requires a separate tayammum for each obligatory prayer because the worshipper must seek water anew for each one. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi prefers a new tayammum for each prayer: God requires seeking water for each prayer, and tayammum is an incomplete necessity-purity that consensus says ends when water appears. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مطرف): A transmission from Ibn al-Qasim through Abu Zayd, and reports from Mutarrif and Ibn al-Majishun, require repeating the second prayer forever because seeking water is a condition. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (كثير من الفقهاء): Many jurists infer that a person without water must first search for it; tayammum becomes permissible after searching and not finding any. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (عائشة): Aisha reports in a sound collection that the Prophet stopped the party at al-Bayda or Dhat al-Jaysh to search for her lost necklace; they had no water, the verse of tayammum came down, and the necklace was found beneath her camel. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Tayammum was legislated in year six during the expedition of al-Muraysiʿ, after the group found itself without water while searching for Aisha's lost necklace. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p318/r3) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p318/r4) supports this position. THALABI (source note THALABI:v3p318/r5) supports this position. IBNATIYYA-FULL (source note IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p58#2/r1) supports this position. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Isḥāq’s search only ahead and nearby, another group’s two bowshots, the Mālikī three-mile view, and al-Shāfiʿī’s limit against losing companions or prayer time; Ibn ʿAṭiyya praises the last view.

question: What does ṣaʿīd mean?

positions.position: The earth's surface
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (ذو الرمة): Dhu al-Rumma’s simile uses saʿid for the earth’s surface, where a fly strikes with its proboscis at midday. TABRISI, d. 548 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says saʿid is the earth’s surface, whether soil or another material, named for the farthest surface one rises to from the earth’s interior. TABRISI, d. 548 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj says linguists agree saʿid is the earth’s surface, supporting the view that tayammum is valid using stone even without soil. TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Saʿid is the earth’s surface without vegetation or trees. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi explains ṣaʿīd as the earth's surface and traces its name to being the upper limit to which one rises. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): If ṣaʿīd means the earth's surface, it is a place where tayammum is performed; if it means soil, it is the direct object with an omitted preposition, and ṭayyib is its adjective or, in the lawful reading, an adverbial or verbal noun. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الخليل): Al-Khalīl says ṣaʿīd is what rises from the earth's surface, meaning the face of the earth. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj defines ṣaʿīd as the earth's surface, whether soil or another material, including bare rock; another scholar adds sand, minerals, and saline earth. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (مالك): Malik interprets sa‘id as anything on the earth’s surface, including soil, sand, trees, stones, and plants. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjaj defines ṣaʿid as the earth’s surface, whether soil or another material, including bare rock. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (الخليل وثعلب): Al-Khalil and Thaʿlab define ṣaʿīd as the earth's surface; al-Zajjaj says linguists do not disagree. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Sa'id means the earth's surface, including stone and soil, so tayammum on a stone is valid even without dust adhering to the hand. STUDYQURAN (al-Ṭabarī): Al-Ṭabarī says ṣaʿīd is any pure or clean part of the earth’s surface; dust adhering to the hands purifies. TAB-FULL (source note TAB-FULL:v7p81/r5) supports this position. question: What does ṭayyib mean?

positions.position: Pure and clean
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Tayyiban means pure. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Tabari allow tayammum on any part of the earth, including soil, sand, stones, minerals, or saline ground; here ṭayyib means pure. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Tayyib means pure. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): Tayyib means thoroughly clean, excluding contaminated or doubtful material. IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): Tayyib means pure, extending the permitted surface material to soil, sand, and stone when free of filth. question: Which materials can be used for tayammum?

positions.position: Materials on or attached to earth may serve
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (مالك): Malik’s Mudawwana prescribes two strikes for tayammum; Ibn al-Jahm says one, and Malik elsewhere says one suffices. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (جمهور المذهب): Most Maliki jurists forbid tayammum on wood, while the Mukhtaṣar of al-Waqqar allows it; the school also differs about plants. IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (مالك): The Mudawwana allows tayammum with snow, while Malik prohibits it in other works. TABRISI, d. 548 (سعيد بن المسيب): A report from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says one strike suffices when tayammum replaces wudu: wipe the face from hairline to nose tip and hands from wrists to fingertips. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The report shows fear, not certainty, suffices; it calls a person who tayammums junub and supports his leading worshippers with ablution, which al-Qurtubi prefers among two Maliki views. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور): Most jurists prohibit tayammum on wood, though Mukhtasar al-Waqqar allows it; one view distinguishes attached from detached wood. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الأوزاعي): Al-Awza'i and al-Thawri allow tayammum on earth and everything on it, including trees, stones, rocks, ice, and snow; al-Tha'labi attributes to Malik permission to strike a tree and wipe with the hand. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (جابر بن عبدالله وابن عمر): Jabir and Ibn Umar transmit from the Prophet that tayammum reaches the elbows; Ibn Umar held this practice. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (مالك والشافعي): Mālik permits minerals for tayammum, while al-Shāfiʿī prohibits them; salt, snow, moved soil, brick, walls, plants, sticks, and trees are disputed. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Tayammum substitutes for wudu as purification, not for every body part: face and hands alone suffice by consensus, though jurists disagree about the method. BURSEVI, d. 1127 (أبو حنيفة): According to Abu Hanifa, striking a bare rock and wiping with it suffices for dry ablution even when it has no dust. positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (أهل المذهب): The Maliki school allows tayammum on both mineral salt and solid salt; other views forbid both or allow mineral salt but forbid solid salt. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet tells Abu Dharr that clean earth is a Muslim's purification even without water for ten years; the opposing jurists treat this as equating soil purification with water ablution. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الخليل): Al-Khalil's lexicon, as cited by Ibn Faris, glosses tayammum with ṣaʿīd as taking its dust, implying soil because smooth stone has no dust. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik and others allow tayammum on minerals, while al-Shafi'i and others prohibit it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Al-Tha'labi says Abu Hanifa permits tayammum with kohl, arsenic, lime, gypsum, and powdered gems, but not metal filings because they are not of the earth's genus. NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 (author): Dry ablution is valid on bare rock even without dust if the person strikes it and wipes with it. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Ibn Kathir recalls Hudhayfa’s report in Muslim that this community’s rows resemble angels’ and that earth is a mosque and its soil purification when water is absent. STUDYQURAN (author): Precious metals and gems are unsuitable as clean earth for tayammum. STUDYQURAN (author): Tayammum requires intention, then two contacts with earth or stone: one to wipe the face, one to wipe the hands.

positions.position: Musk or saffron may serve
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (ابن علية وابن كيسان): Al-Naqqash reports that Ibn ʿUlayya and Ibn Kaysan allowed tayammum with musk and saffron; Ibn ʿAtiyya rejects this as wholly erroneous. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطية): Al-Naqqash reports that Ibn Ulayya and Ibn Kaysan permit tayammum with musk or saffron; Ibn Atiyya calls this completely mistaken. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (ابن علية وابن كيسان): Ibn ʿUlayya and Ibn Kaysān permit tayammum using musk and saffron.

positions.position: Dust-bearing soil is required

question: How many strikes does tayammum require?

positions.position: Two strikes
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (عمار بن ياسر ومكحول والطبري): Ammar and Makhul hold for two strikes, one for the face and one for the hands to the wrists; al-Tabari prefers this view. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (عمار بن ياسر، الزهري): A third view extends wiping from the fingertips to the armpits, citing ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir's report of a travel concession and two strikes, one for the face and one to the shoulders and armpits; al-Zuhrī holds this view. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك والأوزاعي والشافعي وأبو حنيفة والثوري والليث): They require two strikes, one for the face and another for the hands; this method is transmitted from the Prophet by Jabir and Ibn Umar. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن أبي ليلى والحسن بن حي): They require two strikes, each wiping the face, forearms, and elbows. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عمر): Abu ʿUmar resolves conflicting reports by the Qur’an’s apparent wording: two strikes, face then hands to the elbows, by analogy with ablution and following Ibn Umar; a sound Prophetic report would govern. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (مالك وأبو حنيفة والشافعي والثوري والليث وابن أبي سلمة): Mālik in al-Mudawwana, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī, al-Thawrī, al-Layth, and Ibn Abī Salama require two strikes, one for face and one for hands. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (ابن أبي ليلى والحسن): Ibn Abī Laylā and al-Ḥasan also require two strikes, each wiping face, arms, and elbows; Abū Ḥayyān says no other scholar held this. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i’s later position requires two strikes, wiping the face and hands up to the elbows; he argues that ‘hands’ has several ranges and should be read in light of the ablution verse because both concern purification. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن عمر): Al-Daraqutni transmits a marfu‘ report from Ibn Umar prescribing two strikes, one for the face and one for the hands to the elbows; Ibn Kathir rejects its reliability because weak narrators occur in its chains. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (الشافعي): Al-Shafi‘i’s earlier position requires two strikes and wiping the face and hands to the wrists or palms. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عمر): A report raised to the Prophet says tayammum uses two strikes: one for the face and one for the arms up to the elbows. ELMALILI, d. 1361 (author): The practical method is to strike the earth once and wipe the face, then strike again and wipe both hands up to the elbows. positions.position: One strike
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (أكثر الفقهاء وأبو حنيفة والشافعي): Most jurists, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi, and some of al-Tabrisi’s school require one strike, wiping the hands to the elbows. IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (عمار عن النبي): One view limits the hands to the wrists, citing the Prophet's report that tayammum is one strike for the face and palms; this is held by Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, ʿIkrima, al-Awzāʿī, Makḥūl, Mālik, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, and Dāwūd. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن أبي الجهم والأوزاعي وعطاء والشعبي وأحمد بن حنبل وإسحاق وداود والطبري): They hold that tayammum uses one strike; the author calls the report from ʿAmmar the strongest established evidence. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (عمار): A Muslim report from ʿAmmār has the Prophet say one strike on the ground, blowing off dust, then wiping the face and palms suffices. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (عمار): Another Muslim report describes one strike, wiping the left over the right, the backs of the hands, and the face. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (عطاء والشعبي والأوزاعي وأحمد وإسحاق وداود والطبري): The apparent verse and sound reports indicate one strike for face and hands; this is held by ʿAṭāʾ, one report from al-Shaʿbī, al-Awzāʿī's best-known report, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Dāwūd, and al-Ṭabarī. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أحمد): Ahmad’s view is that a single strike suffices to wipe the face and palms, supported by reports from Ammar about the Prophet’s instruction. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عمار): Ammar recalls that he and Umar became junub without water; he rolled in dust and prayed, and the Prophet taught that a single strike of earth, blowing on the hands, and wiping the face and palms sufficed. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (عمار): A separate report from Ammar explicitly states that tayammum is one strike for the face and palms. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو موسى وابن مسعود): Abu Musa reminds Ibn Masud of Ammar’s report that the Prophet taught one strike for the face and hands; Ibn Masud replies that Umar was not persuaded, asks what to do with this verse, and says people might resort to tayammum merely because water feels cold. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (عائشة): Aisha reports that the Prophet demonstrated tayammum with one strike for the face and another for the hands. SUYUTI-LUBAB, d. 911 (الأسلع بن شريك): In al-Ṭabarānī's report, Jibrīl brought the dry-earth verse after al-Aslaʿ told the Prophet he was impure; the Prophet demonstrated one strike for the face and one for the hands to the elbows.

positions.position: A described striking method
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Al-Tabrisi’s school uses that two-strike method when tayammum replaces the major ablution after sexual impurity. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الجمهور): The majority follow the verse's order, wiping the face before the hands; a report in al-Bukhari's chapter on one-strike tayammum mentions the hands first, as do some scholars by analogy with reversing ablution order. DURR-FULL, d. 911 (ابن عمر): Ibn Umar reports the companions struck the earth twice, wiping the face after the first strike and the arms from elbows to wrists after the second. ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (مكحول): Al-Tabari transmits Makḥul's view of a strike for the face and palms through the wrists.

question: What happens when water is found after tayammum?

positions.position: A valid completed prayer need not be repeated
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الشافعي وأبو حنيفة ومالك): Al-Shāfiʿī places tayammum at time's start, Abū Ḥanīfa and others at its end, while Mālik distinguishes the hopeless, hopeful, and uninformed about finding water. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن حبيب): When the chances of finding water or not finding it are equal, delay prayer until the end of the chosen time because water's agreed virtue outweighs the disputed virtue of praying early; Ibn Habib identifies the endpoint. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): If water appears during prayer, Malik says not to interrupt: complete the prayer and use water for later prayers; al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Mundhir agree, while Abu Hanifa, Ahmad, al-Muzani, and others require stopping and restarting. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): There is agreement that finding water before beginning prayer invalidates tayammum and requires using the water. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi cites “do not invalidate your works” as support for completing a prayer begun validly with tayammum; no Sunna or consensus requires cutting it when water appears. IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (أبو ذر): Abu Dharr reports the Prophet saying clean earth purifies a Muslim even without water for ten years; when water is found, one should use it on the skin, which is better. IBNABIHATIM (source note IBNABIHATIM:v3p962/r6) supports this position.

positions.position: Repeat the prayer when water appears
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (أبو علي الجبائي): Al-Jubbaʾi says they must repeat a prayer performed while intoxicated. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn ʿUmar reports that the Prophet delayed ʿIsha while worshippers repeatedly slept and woke, then said only they were waiting for prayer; al-Qurtubi calls it the strongest report by chain and practice. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عبد الملك بن الماجشون): Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun says that if water is found later, the worshipper must repeat the prayer without time limitation. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (طاووس): Tawus, Ata, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Makhul, Ibn Sirin, al-Zuhri, and Rabi'a all say that a person who finds water after the prayer repeats it. QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك وابن نافع): Malik says one strike suffices, whereas Ibn Nafi requires repeating the prayer forever. ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الليث والشافعي): Al-Layth and another report from al-Shāfiʿī allow tayammum and prayer when time would expire, but require repeating after water is found.

question: What is the force of the preposition in wiping?

positions.position: It governs wiping without changing the object
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (author): The preposition باء may govern the verb or be absent without change of meaning; Sībawayh gives مسحت رأسه and مسحت برأسه, and the same alternation with the chest. positions.position: the use of 'prayers' for places of prayer appears in 22:40; the exception for a junub person passing through supports the mosque reading because it permits passage, not prayer there
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The use of 'prayers' for places of prayer appears in 22:40; the exception for a junub person passing through supports the mosque reading because it permits passage, not prayer there. | mentions 22:40

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (قيل): The places-of-prayer interpretation is supported by reading ولا جنبا إلا عابري سبيل as referring to mosques.

positions.position: al-aʿmash reads سكرى with ḍamma on س, on the pattern حبلى, as an adjective of a collective group
positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (الأعمش): Al-Aʿmash reads سكرى with ḍamma on س, on the pattern حبلى, as an adjective of a collective group.

positions.reasons: ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 (عمرو بن مسعود وغيرهما): ʿAmr ibn Masʿūd and others read the phrase as touching by hand; on this view a junub must wash or leave prayer until water is found.

positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (author): سكر with fatḥa on sīn and still kāf means a water barrier; kasra on sīn names the obstructed place, while the form with both vowels open means intoxicating drink, cited in 16:67. | mentions 16:67

positions.position: al-nakha‘i reads سكرى with fatḥa on sīn and still kāf; it may be the same adjective for a group or a broken plural like جرحى, موتى, and هلكى by analogy for affliction; the discussion recalls
positions.reasons: SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 (النخعي): Al-Nakha‘i reads سكرى with fatḥa on sīn and still kāf; it may be the same adjective for a group or a broken plural like جرحى, موتى, and هلكى by analogy for affliction; the discussion recalls 2:85. | mentions 2:85

positions.position: after presenting both views, ibn jarir prefers that the junub person may cross the mosque; reading the exception as a traveler without water would repeat the separate tayammum ruling in 5:6
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (ابن جرير): After presenting both views, Ibn Jarir prefers that the junub person may cross the mosque; reading the exception as a traveler without water would repeat the separate tayammum ruling in 5:6. | mentions 5:6

positions.position: ibn kathir endorses ibn jarir's reading as the majority view and the verse's apparent meaning: it bars prayer in a deficient state and entering its place while junub, except for passage through
positions.reasons: IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 (author): Ibn Kathir endorses Ibn Jarir's reading as the majority view and the verse's apparent meaning: it bars prayer in a deficient state and entering its place while junub, except for passage through.

positions.position: the reading سكارى with fatha is the plural of سكران, like ندمان and ندامى
positions.reasons: ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 (author): The reading سكارى with fatHa is the plural of سكران, like ندمان and ندامى.

positions.position: for those who read prayer as the mosque and travelers as passers through it, the exception clearly removes passers-by from the general prohibition on a junub person’s states
positions.reasons: IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 (author): For those who read prayer as the mosque and travelers as passers through it, the exception clearly removes passers-by from the general prohibition on a junub person’s states.

positions.position: hamza elision in jāʾa with compensatory lengthening yields jā; this is canonical in the seven readings
positions.reasons: QIRAAT-ER (author): Hamza elision in jāʾa with compensatory lengthening yields jā; this is canonical in the Seven readings.

positions.position: this variant softens or elides the initial hamza of aḥad while retaining the hamza of jāʾa
positions.reasons: QIRAAT-ER (author): This variant softens or elides the initial hamza of aḥad while retaining the hamza of jāʾa.

positions.position: eliding hamza at the junction merges the two hamzas into a lengthened ā through canonical phonetic assimilation
positions.reasons: QIRAAT-ER (author): Eliding hamza at the junction merges the two hamzas into a lengthened ā through canonical phonetic assimilation.

positions.position: imāla tilts the fatḥa on jīm toward kasra, producing a sound between ja and ji for certain canonical readers
positions.reasons: QIRAAT-ER (author): Imāla tilts the fatḥa on jīm toward kasra, producing a sound between ja and ji for certain canonical readers.

question: What further question about this verse is addressed?

positions.position: in religious usage, tayammum became the established name for the known act of worship
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (author): In religious usage, tayammum became the established name for the known act of worship. MUJAHID (source note MUJAHID:v1p1/r1) supports this position.

positions.position: al-khalil and others explain ṣaʿīd as the face or surface of the earth; dhu al-rumma’s verse supplies poetic evidence for the term
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الخليل وغيره): Al-Khalil and others explain ṣaʿīd as the face or surface of the earth; Dhu al-Rumma’s verse supplies poetic evidence for the term.

positions.position: malik has two positions in the mudawwana: perform tayammum without repeating, or repeat; in other works he says to obtain water and wash even after sunrise
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (مالك): Malik has two positions in the Mudawwana: perform tayammum without repeating, or repeat; in other works he says to obtain water and wash even after sunrise.

positions.position: if a person tayammums with enough time left for ablution and one rakʿa, some say he must repeat and others say he need not
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (طائفة): If a person tayammums with enough time left for ablution and one rakʿa, some say he must repeat and others say he need not.

positions.position: the verb’s sense of intending is also shown by al-aʿshā of thaʿlaba’s line about heading toward qays
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (author): The verb’s sense of intending is also shown by al-Aʿshā of Thaʿlaba’s line about heading toward Qays.

positions.position: the majority follows the qurʾanic order by wiping the face before the hands; some routes of ʿammar’s hadith in al-bukhari put the hands first, as do scholars reasoning by analogy with reversing ablution order
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الجمهور): The majority follows the Qurʾanic order by wiping the face before the hands; some routes of ʿAmmar’s hadith in al-Bukhari put the hands first, as do scholars reasoning by analogy with reversing ablution order.

positions.position: some permit leaving hard-to-reach folds and the spaces between fingers unwiped, by analogy with folds in leather socks; this is muhammad ibn maslama’s maliki position
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (محمد بن مسلمة): Some permit leaving hard-to-reach folds and the spaces between fingers unwiped, by analogy with folds in leather socks; this is Muhammad ibn Maslama’s Maliki position.

positions.position: one group begins with the left hand, reaches the wrist, continues across that palm, and then repeats on the right, to avoid returning to a limb after moving on
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (طائفة): One group begins with the left hand, reaches the wrist, continues across that palm, and then repeats on the right, to avoid returning to a limb after moving on.

positions.position: another group handles soil in the same manner as water, applying it by a wiping motion but without a prescribed sequence of rank
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (طائفة): Another group handles soil in the same manner as water, applying it by a wiping motion but without a prescribed sequence of rank.

positions.position: al-tabari records four explanations of ṣaʿīd: smooth land, level land, soil, or the face of the earth
positions.reasons: IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 (الطبري): Al-Tabari records four explanations of ṣaʿīd: smooth land, level land, soil, or the face of the earth.

positions.position: one answer says some intoxication leaves enough reason for commands; another says the prohibition is against exposing oneself to intoxication when prayer is due
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): One answer says some intoxication leaves enough reason for commands; another says the prohibition is against exposing oneself to intoxication when prayer is due.

positions.position: after commanding worship in the previous verse, god next mentions prayer as one of the greatest acts of worship
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): After commanding worship in the previous verse, God next mentions prayer as one of the greatest acts of worship.

positions.position: one interpretation is do not perform prayer while intoxicated
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وابن زيد): One interpretation is do not perform prayer while intoxicated.

positions.position: the condition means discerning what one says; another explanation is retaining what one recites from the quran
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): The condition means discerning what one says; another explanation is retaining what one recites from the Quran.

positions.position: one report says the verse was revealed about an ill man from the ansar who could not rise to perform ablution
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): One report says the verse was revealed about an ill man from the Ansar who could not rise to perform ablution.

positions.position: al-baqir and al-sadiq are reported to permit tayammum in all the foregoing circumstances
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (السيدان الباقر والصادق): Al-Baqir and al-Sadiq are reported to permit tayammum in all the foregoing circumstances.

positions.position: the phrase means that you are travelers
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): The phrase means that you are travelers.

positions.position: the verse shows that a drunk person’s prayer is invalid
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): The verse shows that a drunk person’s prayer is invalid.

positions.position: consensus requires the intoxicated person to make up the prayer
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Consensus requires the intoxicated person to make up the prayer.

positions.position: another gloss takes ṭayyib as productive soil, contrasted with barren salt land, as in 7:58
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Another gloss takes ṭayyib as productive soil, contrasted with barren salt land, as in 7:58. | mentions 7:58

positions.position: god accepts the concession of tayammum in place of wudu, making the obligation easier
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): God accepts the concession of tayammum in place of wudu, making the obligation easier.

positions.position: the cited verse’s explanation says talmas means seek
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (الشاعر): The cited verse’s explanation says talmas means seek.

positions.position: al-asha’s verse uses tayaammamtu to mean that he set out for or intended qays despite rugged country between
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (الأعشى): Al-Asha’s verse uses tayaammamtu to mean that he set out for or intended Qays despite rugged country between.

positions.position: a second cited verse uses tayaammamtu to mean intending a home
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (الشاعر): A second cited verse uses tayaammamtu to mean intending a home.

positions.position: qaraba can be transitive or intransitive; qurb al-maʾ means to approach or reach water
positions.reasons: TABRISI, d. 548 (author): Qaraba can be transitive or intransitive; qurb al-maʾ means to approach or reach water.

positions.position: the qur'anic list includes ب as a particle that completes the expression; examples include wiping the face, wiping the head, and growing with oil
positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 (بعض المفسرين): The Qur'anic list includes ب as a particle that completes the expression; examples include wiping the face, wiping the head, and growing with oil. | mentions 5:6, 23:20

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (الضحاك): Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the intoxication is from sleep; the author considers this far-fetched.

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (author): One explanation for the term is that semen has moved away from its proper place.

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (author): The “or” functions like “and”; otherwise the sick and traveler would owe purification even without the occurrence of ritual impurity.

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (مجاهد): Mujāhid says the verse came down after a sick Anṣārī man unable to rise for ablution and without a servant asked the Prophet for help.

positions.reasons: IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 (الشافعي): Al-Shāfiʿī says the name al-ṣaʿīd applies only to soil that has dust.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الواحدي): Al-Wāḥidī says sukkārā is the plural of sakrān; adjectives on faʿlān take the plural patterns fuʿālā and fuʿālā, as in kasālā.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): Rāzī answers that divine seeking is figurative: God singled out Muḥammad and commanded people, whose failure is like seeking something and not finding it.

positions.position: there is consensus that someone who has water but needs it for their own thirst or that of a protected animal may perform tayammum
positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (author): There is consensus that someone who has water but needs it for their own thirst or that of a protected animal may perform tayammum.

positions.reasons: RAZI-FULL, d. 606 (الزجاج): Al-Zajjāj explains ṣaʿīd as the face of the earth, whether soil or another material.

positions.position: abū dāwūd grades the report about janāba under every hair weak; al-ḥārith ibn wajīh is weak and his reports are rejected, so the author rejects it as proof

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (محمد بن عبد الحكم وأبو الفرج): Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Ḥakam holds that pouring suffices; Abū al-Faraj later returned to this position and transmitted it from Mālik.

positions.position: marwān ibn muḥammad al-ẓāhirī, described as trustworthy, says mālik ruled valid a junub's prayer after immersion without ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مروان بن محمد الظاهري): Marwān ibn Muḥammad al-Ẓāhirī, described as trustworthy, says Mālik ruled valid a junub's prayer after immersion without ablution.

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عبد البر): Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr says the report of Ibn ʿAbbās washing his hands and genitals seven times is countered by the reports of ʿĀʾisha and Maymūna.

positions.position: saḥnūn says someone unable to rub their own body should have another person do it or use a cloth
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (سحنون): Saḥnūn says someone unable to rub their own body should have another person do it or use a cloth.

positions.position: al-wāḍiḥa says to rub the accessible parts of the body, then pour water over the rest until all of it is covered
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الواضحة): Al-Wāḍiḥa says to rub the accessible parts of the body, then pour water over the rest until all of it is covered.

positions.position: those who do not require the rinses argue that scripture and the prophet do not command them and there is no consensus; obligations require such proof
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (من لم يوجبهما): Those who do not require the rinses argue that scripture and the Prophet do not command them and there is no consensus; obligations require such proof.

positions.position: muḥammad ibn ʿīsā al-aʿshā says a farq equals three ṣāʿs, or five qisṭs and twelve prophetic mudd measures; sufyān likewise says it is three ṣāʿs
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (محمد بن عيسى الأعشى): Muḥammad ibn ʿĪsā al-Aʿshā says a farq equals three ṣāʿs, or five qisṭs and twelve Prophetic mudd measures; Sufyān likewise says it is three ṣāʿs.

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): These reports recommend using only the water needed, without fixed measure; excess is wasteful and blameworthy, while the author calls the Ibāḍī practice of using much water satanic.

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك والشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور): This group supports requiring intention with the command to worship sincerely in 98:5 and the Prophet's statement that actions depend on intentions. | mentions 98:5

positions.position: ibn wahb defines a farq as a wooden measure; ibn shihāb said it held five umayyad measures called qisṭs
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن وهب): Ibn Wahb defines a farq as a wooden measure; Ibn Shihāb said it held five Umayyad measures called qisṭs.

positions.position: the searchers found nothing on their route, but when they returned and raised the camel, they found the necklace beneath it

positions.position: al-bukhārī gives no location and names asmāʾ as owner, unlike mālik's account naming ʿāʾisha

positions.position: al-tirmidhī's report says the necklace fell at al-abwāʾ and the prophet sent two men to search for it

positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The Prophet surprised Banu al-Mustaliq at al-Muraysiʿ while they were unaware, taking captives; their battle cry was Amit amit.

positions.position: another account says banu al-mustaliq had assembled to attack the prophet, who went out to meet them after hearing of it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Another account says Banu al-Mustaliq had assembled to attack the Prophet, who went out to meet them after hearing of it.

positions.position: illness is the body's departure from its ordinary, balanced condition; it may be severe or slight
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Illness is the body's departure from its ordinary, balanced condition; it may be severe or slight.

positions.position: the other maliki view bars a tayammum imam from leading people with ablution because the imam should have the higher ritual rank
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The other Maliki view bars a tayammum imam from leading people with ablution because the imam should have the higher ritual rank.

positions.position: a report from jabir says a tayammum imam must not lead worshippers who have ablution; al-daraqutni grades its chain weak
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (جابر بن عبد الله): A report from Jabir says a tayammum imam must not lead worshippers who have ablution; al-Daraqutni grades its chain weak.

positions.position: al-daraqutni says the jabir wound report is weak through al-zubayr b. khurayq; al-awzaʿi's ibn ʿabbas route is the sounder version, while another route is mursal. ibn abi hatim records a musnad route
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الدارقطني): Al-Daraqutni says the Jabir wound report is weak through al-Zubayr b. Khurayq; al-Awzaʿi's Ibn ʿAbbas route is the sounder version, while another route is mursal. Ibn Abi Hatim records a musnad route.

positions.position: those who exclude healthy residents argue that the text conditioned this concession on illness or travel, like fasting exemption and shortened prayer
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Those who exclude healthy residents argue that the text conditioned this concession on illness or travel, like fasting exemption and shortened prayer.

positions.position: al-zuhri reads al-ghayt; al-qurtubi says it may be a lightened form of al-ghayt or a y-for-waw reversal from al-ghawt
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الزهري): Al-Zuhri reads al-ghayt; al-Qurtubi says it may be a lightened form of al-ghayt or a y-for-waw reversal from al-ghawt.

positions.position: ahmad says light sleep does not matter if it neither penetrates nor overwhelms the heart
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد بن حنبل): Ahmad says light sleep does not matter if it neither penetrates nor overwhelms the heart.

positions.position: abu hanifa and his companions require ablution only for someone sleeping on a side or sitting with weight shifted
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة وأصحابه): Abu Hanifa and his companions require ablution only for someone sleeping on a side or sitting with weight shifted.

positions.position: al-shafiʿi says sitting sleep does not invalidate ablution; ibn wahb also transmits this from malik
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi says sitting sleep does not invalidate ablution; Ibn Wahb also transmits this from Malik.

positions.position: al-qurtubi considers malik's well-known position the soundest of these views
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Al-Qurtubi considers Malik's well-known position the soundest of these views.

positions.position: muslims agree that fainting, insanity, and intoxication, as losses of reason, require ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Muslims agree that fainting, insanity, and intoxication, as losses of reason, require ablution.

positions.position: sleep has three positions: it is itself an invalidator, never an invalidator without another event, or a middle case based on its depth or posture
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Sleep has three positions: it is itself an invalidator, never an invalidator without another event, or a middle case based on its depth or posture.

positions.position: al-muzani treats any amount of sleep as an invalidator; this is implied by malik's muwatta wording and by the safwan report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (المزني أبو إبراهيم إسماعيل): Al-Muzani treats any amount of sleep as an invalidator; this is implied by Malik's Muwatta wording and by the Safwan report.

positions.position: safwan reports the prophet allowed wiping over the khuffs after urine, stool, or sleep, removing them only for janaba; al-qurtubi says al-tirmidhi authenticated the report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (صفوان بن عسال المرادي): Safwan reports the Prophet allowed wiping over the khuffs after urine, stool, or sleep, removing them only for janaba; al-Qurtubi says al-Tirmidhi authenticated the report.

positions.position: proponents equate sleep with urine and stool because deep sleep overwhelms reason; they also cite ali's general report that sleep loosens the anal tether and requires ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Proponents equate sleep with urine and stool because deep sleep overwhelms reason; they also cite Ali's general report that sleep loosens the anal tether and requires ablution.

positions.position: abu musa regarded sleep as no invalidator at all unless another event occurred; he would sleep under guard and pray on waking, as did ʿubayda, saʿid b. al-musayyab, and al-awzaʿi in one report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو موسى الأشعري): Abu Musa regarded sleep as no invalidator at all unless another event occurred; he would sleep under guard and pray on waking, as did ʿUbayda, Saʿid b. al-Musayyab, and al-Awzaʿi in one report.

positions.position: malik requires ablution after deep, prolonged sleep in any posture; al-zuhri, rabiʿa, and al-awzaʿi in one narration agree
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Malik requires ablution after deep, prolonged sleep in any posture; al-Zuhri, Rabiʿa, and al-Awzaʿi in one narration agree.

positions.position: al-qurtubi interprets malik's and safwan's references to sleep as heavy sleep that dominates the sleeper, in light of ibn ʿumar's report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi interprets Malik's and Safwan's references to sleep as heavy sleep that dominates the sleeper, in light of Ibn ʿUmar's report.

positions.position: wakiʿ's safwan route says or wind instead of or sleep; daraqutni says no one else transmits that wording, and wakiʿ is trustworthy, weakening the use of safwan as proof that sleep itself invalidates ablution
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (وكيع): Wakiʿ's Safwan route says or wind instead of or sleep; Daraqutni says no one else transmits that wording, and Wakiʿ is trustworthy, weakening the use of Safwan as proof that sleep itself invalidates ablution.

positions.position: a report from ibn ʿabbas says the prophet slept prostrating, then said only side-sleep relaxes the joints and requires ablution; al-daraqutni, abu dawud, and abu ʿumar call it unsound or munkar
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): A report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet slept prostrating, then said only side-sleep relaxes the joints and requires ablution; al-Daraqutni, Abu Dawud, and Abu ʿUmar call it unsound or munkar.

positions.position: al-shafiʿi, al-tabari, and dawud require ablution after sleep in any position except sitting, which is unlikely to become deep; this is also reported from ali, ibn masʿud, and ibn ʿumar
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi, al-Tabari, and Dawud require ablution after sleep in any position except sitting, which is unlikely to become deep; this is also reported from Ali, Ibn Masʿud, and Ibn ʿUmar.

positions.position: ʿamr b. shuʿayb transmits a prophetic report distinguishing sitting sleep, which does not require ablution, from lying on one's side, which does
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمرو بن شعيب): ʿAmr b. Shuʿayb transmits a prophetic report distinguishing sitting sleep, which does not require ablution, from lying on one's side, which does.

positions.position: the prophet directed worshippers to begin eating when dinner is served at the time prayer is called, removing a distraction so they can approach worship with an unoccupied, humble heart
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet directed worshippers to begin eating when dinner is served at the time prayer is called, removing a distraction so they can approach worship with an unoccupied, humble heart.

positions.position: the passage follows the command to worship god alone in 4:36 by discussing prayer, the foremost act of worship, its obligation, and the conditions required for validity
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The passage follows the command to worship God alone in 4:36 by discussing prayer, the foremost act of worship, its obligation, and the conditions required for validity. | mentions 4:36

positions.position: al-shafi'i takes 'prayer' to mean its place, the mosque, with an omitted word understood
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafi'i takes 'prayer' to mean its place, the mosque, with an omitted word understood.

positions.position: ubayda al-salmani interprets the phrase as being in need of urination, supported by the prohibition on praying while needing to urinate or while squeezing one's thighs
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عبيدة السلماني): Ubayda al-Salmani interprets the phrase as being in need of urination, supported by the prohibition on praying while needing to urinate or while squeezing one's thighs.

positions.position: the report says a person who sleeps sitting does not need ablution, but one who lies down does
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمرو بن شعيب): The report says a person who sleeps sitting does not need ablution, but one who lies down does.

positions.position: bukhari reports that a wife of the prophet in retreat saw blood and yellow discharge beneath her while praying; al-qurtubi treats it as an abnormal, illness-related discharge
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): Bukhari reports that a wife of the Prophet in retreat saw blood and yellow discharge beneath her while praying; al-Qurtubi treats it as an abnormal, illness-related discharge.

positions.position: malik does not make this unusual outlet obligatorily invalidate ablution, unlike al-shafiʿi; this supports malik's distinction from the hanafi rule based on impurity alone
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Malik does not make this unusual outlet obligatorily invalidate ablution, unlike al-Shafiʿi; this supports Malik's distinction from the Hanafi rule based on impurity alone.

positions.position: al-shafiʿi requires ablution when any part of a man's body contacts a woman's body without a barrier, regardless of desire; this is also attributed to ibn masʿud, ibn ʿumar, al-zuhri, and rabiʿa
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafiʿi requires ablution when any part of a man's body contacts a woman's body without a barrier, regardless of desire; this is also attributed to Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Zuhri, and Rabiʿa.

positions.position: although malikis accept mursal reports in principle, al-qurtubi rejects this one because the verse's apparent sense and the companions' practice oppose it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Although Malikis accept mursal reports in principle, al-Qurtubi rejects this one because the verse's apparent sense and the Companions' practice oppose it.

positions.position: al-marwazi says only malik and al-layth require ablution when pleasure comes through clothing; al-qurtubi adds that ibn ʿabd al-barr also attributes this rule to ishaq and ahmad and reports it from other early authorities
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (المروزي): Al-Marwazi says only Malik and al-Layth require ablution when pleasure comes through clothing; al-Qurtubi adds that Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr also attributes this rule to Ishaq and Ahmad and reports it from other early authorities.

positions.position: a sound report from ʿaisha says the prophet nudged her feet when they lay before him during prayer; they had no lamps, and bukhari records the report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): A sound report from ʿAisha says the Prophet nudged her feet when they lay before him during prayer; they had no lamps, and Bukhari records the report.

positions.position: al-qurtubi says ghamz is pressing with the hand, like feeling a ram to test whether it is fat, not striking someone with a sleeve
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi says ghamz is pressing with the hand, like feeling a ram to test whether it is fat, not striking someone with a sleeve.

positions.position: aisha describes the prophet moving her legs when he prostrated and her extending them again when he stood; qurtubi treats this as direct contact without an intervening barrier
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عائشة): Aisha describes the Prophet moving her legs when he prostrated and her extending them again when he stood; Qurtubi treats this as direct contact without an intervening barrier.

positions.position: al-muzani proposes that a barrier covered the prophet's foot; qurtubi rejects this because the default is direct contact unless a barrier is established
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (المزني): Al-Muzani proposes that a barrier covered the Prophet's foot; Qurtubi rejects this because the default is direct contact unless a barrier is established.

positions.position: qurtubi says the alleged consensus is disputed because al-a'mash and others disagreed; even if granted, it begs the question, while sound reports support his position
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi says the alleged consensus is disputed because al-A'mash and others disagreed; even if granted, it begs the question, while sound reports support his position.

positions.position: qurtubi invokes the maxim to follow an authenticated report over one's own opinion, noting malik, al-shafi'i's teacher, was already known to say it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi invokes the maxim to follow an authenticated report over one's own opinion, noting Malik, al-Shafi'i's teacher, was already known to say it.

positions.position: the prophet carried umama, daughter of zaynab, during prayer, setting her down for bowing and lifting her after prostration
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet carried Umama, daughter of Zaynab, during prayer, setting her down for bowing and lifting her after prostration.

positions.position: when water is likely to appear, malik's companions report delaying prayer to mid-time in hope of water, provided the delay does not forfeit the virtue of praying early
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): When water is likely to appear, Malik's companions report delaying prayer to mid-time in hope of water, provided the delay does not forfeit the virtue of praying early.

positions.position: qurtubi says pleasure is the criterion: wherever pleasure occurs, the ruling of required ablution follows; he contrasts this with al-shafi'i's treatment of unmarriageable kin
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi says pleasure is the criterion: wherever pleasure occurs, the ruling of required ablution follows; he contrasts this with al-Shafi'i's treatment of unmarriageable kin.

positions.position: someone who knows water will be available at the end of the time may pray with tayammum early, but must repeat within the time if water later appears
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن القاسم): Ibn al-Qasim says that someone who knows water will be available at the end of the time may pray with tayammum early, but must repeat within the time if water later appears.

positions.position: the report that ibn mas'ud performed ablution with nabidh is not established because its narrator abu zayd is unknown and not known as a companion of abdullah, according to ibn al-mundhir and others
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن المنذر): The report that Ibn Mas'ud performed ablution with nabidh is not established because its narrator Abu Zayd is unknown and not known as a companion of Abdullah, according to Ibn al-Mundhir and others.

positions.position: the water whose absence permits tayammum is pure and purifying water that remains in its original qualities
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The water whose absence permits tayammum is pure and purifying water that remains in its original qualities.

positions.position: al-shafi'i's other opinion requires using the water at hand and then performing tayammum for the part left without water, since the person initially possessed water
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): Al-Shafi'i's other opinion requires using the water at hand and then performing tayammum for the part left without water, since the person initially possessed water.

positions.position: on forgetting water in one's baggage and using tayammum, al-shafi'i's sounder view requires repeating because the water was present and the person was negligent; another view, also attributed to malik, waives repetition if it was
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): On forgetting water in one's baggage and using tayammum, al-Shafi'i's sounder view requires repeating because the water was present and the person was negligent; another view, also attributed to Malik, waives repetition if it was unknown.

positions.position: abu hanifa permits ablution with water whose qualities have changed, arguing that the indefinite “water” in the verse is linguistically general
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو حنيفة): Abu Hanifa permits ablution with water whose qualities have changed, arguing that the indefinite “water” in the verse is linguistically general.

positions.position: qurtubi answers that the generality covers kinds within the genus of water, such as rain, rivers, springs, fresh, and salt water, not other liquids such as bean or rose water
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi answers that the generality covers kinds within the genus of water, such as rain, rivers, springs, fresh, and salt water, not other liquids such as bean or rose water.

positions.position: the kufans, including abu hanifa and his followers, argue that date nabidh counts as water and prevents tayammum; qurtubi says their supporting reports are weak and treats the issue later in al-furqan
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الكوفيون): The Kufans, including Abu Hanifa and his followers, argue that date nabidh counts as water and prevents tayammum; Qurtubi says their supporting reports are weak and treats the issue later in al-Furqan.

positions.position: ibn al-sikkit glosses the quranic command as “aim” or “intend”; repeated usage then made the word denote wiping face and hands with soil
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن السكيت): Ibn al-Sikkit glosses the Quranic command as “aim” or “intend”; repeated usage then made the word denote wiping face and hands with soil.

positions.position: imru al-qays uses tayammam for heading toward a destination, in two poems about traveling toward a place and a spring
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (امرؤ القيس): Imru al-Qays uses tayammam for heading toward a destination, in two poems about traveling toward a place and a spring.

positions.position: an unnamed poet uses the verb for directing a camel toward another country when dissatisfied with the current land
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (آخر): An unnamed poet uses the verb for directing a camel toward another country when dissatisfied with the current land.

positions.position: al-a'sha of bahila's verse uses tayammam for setting out toward qays across difficult terrain
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أعشى باهلة): Al-A'sha of Bahila's verse uses tayammam for setting out toward Qays across difficult terrain.

positions.position: hamid ibn thawr's verse uses the verb to ask where someone directed herself, illustrating its sense of intending or setting out
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (حميد بن ثور): Hamid ibn Thawr's verse uses the verb to ask where someone directed herself, illustrating its sense of intending or setting out.

positions.position: two cited verses use mayammam for a person who directs himself toward a noble house, illustrating the word's sense of aiming or being directed
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Two cited verses use mayammam for a person who directs himself toward a noble house, illustrating the word's sense of aiming or being directed.

positions.position: the rule to perform tayammum and pray wherever prayer catches a person is al-shafi'i's and ahmad's view, and is also reported from ali, ibn umar, and ibn abbas
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشافعي): The rule to perform tayammum and pray wherever prayer catches a person is al-Shafi'i's and Ahmad's view, and is also reported from Ali, Ibn Umar, and Ibn Abbas.

positions.position: ibn abd al-barr calls abu salama's reports contradictory and poorly considered, adding that abu salama was not as learned as his medinan successor peers
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عبد البر): Ibn Abd al-Barr calls Abu Salama's reports contradictory and poorly considered, adding that Abu Salama was not as learned as his Medinan Successor peers.

positions.position: al-qaffal suggests that the permitted drink may have been only enough to stir generosity, bravery, and spirited honor
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (القفال): Al-Qaffal suggests that the permitted drink may have been only enough to stir generosity, bravery, and spirited honor.

positions.position: hassan's line 'we drink it and it makes us kings' is cited as poetic evidence for the drink's association with generosity and courage
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (حسان): Hassan's line 'we drink it and it makes us kings' is cited as poetic evidence for the drink's association with generosity and courage.

positions.position: al-qaffal says deliberately drinking enough to remove reason into insanity or unconsciousness was not permitted; if this happened unintentionally, the person is excused, a position al-qurtubi affirms
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (القفال): Al-Qaffal says deliberately drinking enough to remove reason into insanity or unconsciousness was not permitted; if this happened unintentionally, the person is excused, a position al-Qurtubi affirms.

positions.position: after this verse, muslims avoided drink at prayer times but drank after the night prayer until wine was prohibited in 5:91
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): After this verse, Muslims avoided drink at prayer times but drank after the night prayer until wine was prohibited in 5:91. | mentions 5:91

positions.position: intoxication is the opposite of sobriety; the verb means to become intoxicated, an eye can become bewildered, and a crack can be blocked. the drunk person is cut off from his former reason
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Intoxication is the opposite of sobriety; the verb means to become intoxicated, an eye can become bewildered, and a crack can be blocked. The drunk person is cut off from his former reason. | mentions 15:15

positions.position: al-qurtubi says the verse plainly shows drinking was permitted in early islam until it brought the drinker to intoxication
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Al-Qurtubi says the verse plainly shows drinking was permitted in early Islam until it brought the drinker to intoxication.

positions.position: some say intoxication is rationally forbidden and was never permitted by any religion, so they interpret the verse's intoxication as sleep
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (قوم): Some say intoxication is rationally forbidden and was never permitted by any religion, so they interpret the verse's intoxication as sleep.

positions.position: by analogy, someone fasting most of an expiation fast does not discard it upon finding an enslaved person to free; likewise, one who began prayer with tayammum completes it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): By analogy, someone fasting most of an expiation fast does not discard it upon finding an enslaved person to free; likewise, one who began prayer with tayammum completes it.

positions.position: al-kiya al-tabari says al-shafi'i requires dust to adhere to the hand and be transferred to the body parts, analogizing earth to water; he admits ṣaʿīd alone does not prove this restriction
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الكيا الطبري): Al-Kiya al-Tabari says al-Shafi'i requires dust to adhere to the hand and be transferred to the body parts, analogizing earth to water; he admits ṣaʿīd alone does not prove this restriction.

positions.position: qurtubi rejects treating the hadith naming soil as a restriction on the general earth term, comparing it to a verse that names dates and pomegranates among fruits
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi rejects treating the hadith naming soil as a restriction on the general earth term, comparing it to a verse that names dates and pomegranates among fruits.

positions.position: dhu al-rumma's verse uses ṣaʿīd for the ground, describing an insect striking it with its snout
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ذو الرمة): Dhu al-Rumma's verse uses ṣaʿīd for the ground, describing an insect striking it with its snout.

positions.position: ṣaʿīd has the plural ṣaʿidat; the hadith warning against sitting in public roads uses that plural
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Ṣaʿīd has the plural ṣaʿidat; the hadith warning against sitting in public roads uses that plural.

positions.position: qurtubi's analogy also points to the al-baqara verse listing angels, messengers, gabriel, and michael, where naming examples does not restrict the broader class
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): Qurtubi's analogy also points to the al-Baqara verse listing angels, messengers, Gabriel, and Michael, where naming examples does not restrict the broader class. | mentions 2:98

positions.position: the prophet tells a junub person to use ṣaʿīd because it suffices; qurtubi cites this to support the earth-surface interpretation
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم): The Prophet tells a junub person to use ṣaʿīd because it suffices; Qurtubi cites this to support the earth-surface interpretation.

positions.position: ibn khuwayz mindad says malik permits tayammum on grass if it lies beneath the earth
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن خويز منداد): Ibn Khuwayz Mindad says Malik permits tayammum on grass if it lies beneath the earth.

positions.position: maliki sources differ on snow: the mudawwana and al-mabsut allow it, while other sources prohibit it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (مالك): Maliki sources differ on snow: the Mudawwana and al-Mabsut allow it, while other sources prohibit it.

positions.position: abu umar says the scholars generally allow tayammum on saline ground, with ishaq ibn rahawayh the exception
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو عمر): Abu Umar says the scholars generally allow tayammum on saline ground, with Ishaq ibn Rahawayh the exception.

positions.position: ibn abbas says a person who reaches the point of tayammum while in mud should coat part of the body with mud and, once dry, use it for tayammum
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): Ibn Abbas says a person who reaches the point of tayammum while in mud should coat part of the body with mud and, once dry, use it for tayammum.

positions.position: the author judges the one-strike report from ʿammar the strongest established evidence about the number of strikes
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عمار): The author judges the one-strike report from ʿAmmar the strongest established evidence about the number of strikes.

positions.position: when abu ishaq mentioned the elbow report from ʿammar, ahmad admired it
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد بن حنبل): When Abu Ishaq mentioned the elbow report from ʿAmmar, Ahmad admired it.

positions.position: ibn ʿatiyya says the armpit view lacks evidence; others infer from the general word ‘hand,’ analogy with ablution, wrist reports, analogy with amputation, or ʿammar’s palm report
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عطية): Ibn ʿAtiyya says the armpit view lacks evidence; others infer from the general word ‘hand,’ analogy with ablution, wrist reports, analogy with amputation, or ʿAmmar’s palm report. | mentions 5:38

positions.position: ibn shas locates the disagreement in the muddled person who retains some reason; one wholly unable to distinguish heaven from earth or man from woman is unanimously treated as insane, except some say missed prayer
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن شاس): Ibn Shas locates the disagreement in the muddled person who retains some reason; one wholly unable to distinguish heaven from earth or man from woman is unanimously treated as insane, except some say missed prayer remains due because intoxication was self-induced.

positions.position: ahmad defines intoxication as a change from sound reason, and a similar view is related from malik
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أحمد ومالك): Ahmad defines intoxication as a change from sound reason, and a similar view is related from Malik.

positions.position: al-farra says one may say that a man became junub or ajnaba
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الفراء): Al-Farra says one may say that a man became junub or ajnaba.

positions.position: abu yusuf and al-shafi'i consider the drunk apostate an apostate, although al-shafi'i would not kill him or call on him to repent while intoxicated
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (أبو يوسف والشافعي): Abu Yusuf and al-Shafi'i consider the drunk apostate an apostate, although al-Shafi'i would not kill him or call on him to repent while intoxicated.

positions.position: an ʿabr-asfār camel is one that repeatedly crosses deserts and hot midday terrain because it walks quickly
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): An ʿabr-asfār camel is one that repeatedly crosses deserts and hot midday terrain because it walks quickly.

positions.position: the poet's line depicts a swift camel traversing the heat, illustrating the travel sense of ʿabr
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (الشاعر): The poet's line depicts a swift camel traversing the heat, illustrating the travel sense of ʿabr.

positions.position: the expression ʿabara al-qawm means that the people died; the accompanying poem contrasts dying with surviving until death
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The expression ʿabara al-qawm means that the people died; the accompanying poem contrasts dying with surviving until death.

positions.position: the poem means that if the people die they have peers, while if they survive they remain destined to die
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The poem means that if the people die they have peers, while if they survive they remain destined to die.

positions.position: ibn ʿabbās, ibn masʿūd, ʿikrima, and al-nakhaʿī interpret the exception as someone passing through, as do ʿamr ibn dīnār, mālik, and al-shāfiʿī
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس وابن مسعود وعكرمة والنخعي): Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿIkrima, and al-Nakhaʿī interpret the exception as someone passing through, as do ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, Mālik, and al-Shāfiʿī.

positions.position: a report in ṣaḥīḥ muslim has the prophet order that every small opening into the mosque be closed except abū bakr's
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (النبي): A report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim has the Prophet order that every small opening into the mosque be closed except Abū Bakr's.

positions.position: the order blocked using the mosque as a passage; abū bakr's opening was excepted as an honor because he and the prophet were usually together
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The order blocked using the mosque as a passage; Abū Bakr's opening was excepted as an honor because he and the Prophet were usually together.

positions.position: ibn ʿumar points to the prophet's house and ʿalī's adjacent house, saying no other houses were in the mosque
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn ʿUmar points to the Prophet's house and ʿAlī's adjacent house, saying no other houses were in the mosque.

positions.position: ʿamr ibn maymūn reports from ibn ʿabbās that the prophet ordered all doors closed except ʿalī's
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عباس): ʿAmr ibn Maymūn reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the Prophet ordered all doors closed except ʿAlī's.

positions.position: the author distinguishes the small windows or openings called khukhāt from ʿalī's ordinary entrance door and abū bakr's opening
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (author): The author distinguishes the small windows or openings called khukhāt from ʿAlī's ordinary entrance door and Abū Bakr's opening.

positions.position: ibn ʿumar's statement that only the prophet's and ʿalī's houses were in the mosque explains their household access
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): Ibn ʿUmar's statement that only the Prophet's and ʿAlī's houses were in the mosque explains their household access.

positions.position: the author's scholars generally prohibit a junub from reciting qur'an, allowing only a few short verses for seeking protection
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علماؤنا): The author's scholars generally prohibit a junub from reciting Qur'an, allowing only a few short verses for seeking protection.

positions.position: a report from ibn ʿumar attributes to the prophet a prohibition on any qur'anic recitation by a junub or menstruating woman
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (ابن عمر): A report from Ibn ʿUmar attributes to the Prophet a prohibition on any Qur'anic recitation by a junub or menstruating woman.

positions.position: ʿalī reports that nothing kept the prophet from reciting qur'an except janāba; shuʿba praised the report and the author calls its chain sound
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (علي): ʿAlī reports that nothing kept the Prophet from reciting Qur'an except janāba; Shuʿba praised the report and the author calls its chain sound.

positions.position: a report from ʿabd allāh ibn rawāḥa says the prophet forbade reciting qur'an while junub
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عبد الله بن رواحة): A report from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa says the Prophet forbade reciting Qur'an while junub.

positions.position: ʿikrima recounts ibn rawāḥa's wife finding him with a slave girl; he recites verses to show he is not junub, she trusts god over her sight, and the prophet later smiles at the story
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (عكرمة): ʿIkrima recounts Ibn Rawāḥa's wife finding him with a slave girl; he recites verses to show he is not junub, she trusts God over her sight, and the Prophet later smiles at the story.

positions.position: said ibn jubayr says early muslims drank after 2:219, arguing the benefit made it permissible; a drunken prayer leader mangled al-kafirun, prompting this verse, then 5:91 ended drinking and umar declared they had stopped
positions.reasons: QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 (سعيد بن جبير): Said ibn Jubayr says early Muslims drank after 2:219, arguing the benefit made it permissible; a drunken prayer leader mangled al-Kafirun, prompting this verse, then 5:91 ended drinking and Umar declared they had stopped. | mentions 2:219, 5:91, 109:2

positions.position: the ḥanafīs allow striking hard stone, while al-bayḍāwī’s school requires dust to adhere; min in the cited verse is partitive, and treating it as a starting point is strained
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The Ḥanafīs allow striking hard stone, while al-Bayḍāwī’s school requires dust to adhere; min in the cited verse is partitive, and treating it as a starting point is strained.

positions.position: do not enter prayer while intoxicated through sleep or wine until sober and understanding what you say in prayer
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): Do not enter prayer while intoxicated through sleep or wine until sober and understanding what you say in prayer.

positions.position: the phrase marks the end of the prohibition for a junub person; it also teaches worshippers to avoid distractions and purify the soul
positions.reasons: BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 (author): The phrase marks the end of the prohibition for a junub person; it also teaches worshippers to avoid distractions and purify the soul.
